Its question has aged well: once you can do something remarkable, what responsibility follows? Heroes works because it makes that question personal before anyone gets to call themselves a hero.

title: Who Is a Football Club For? What Ted Lasso and Manchester City Reveal About Ownership
description: Ted Lasso trusts a good owner to protect football. Manchester City's financial ruling asks what happens when trust is not enough.
body: In Ted Lasso 's third season, Edwin Akufo gathers club owners to sell them a lucrative new league. Rebecca Welton looks around the room and asks them to remember the people who first made them love football. Her argument works. The other owners abandon the scheme, and the game is saved from their worst instincts by one of their own. It is an appealing scene, especially because Rebecca once treated AFC Richmond as a tool for hurting her ex-husband. She has learned to care about the club and the people around it. Still, the decision happens in a room full of owners. Supporters are central to Rebecca's argument, but none of them gets a seat at the table. The club is theirs in feeling and hers in law. That gap between belonging and control is where Ted Lasso has something to say about real football. Manchester City's newly published financial ruling makes the limits of the show's answer easier to see. Richmond and City are not equivalent clubs, and Edwin Akufo's fictional league has nothing to do with the charges against City. The connection is the power that ownership gives someone over a competition other people have built their lives around. Spoilers for Ted Lasso through season three follow. Rebecca's change is the point In the pilot, Rebecca hires Ted because she expects him to fail. Richmond's staff, players and fans face the consequences of a plan they know nothing about. Her ownership gives her the freedom to try it. As the series continues, Ted helps create a culture in which players support each other and staff members are heard. Rebecca begins to value that culture herself. The season-three episode "International Break" takes her change beyond Richmond. Akufo's proposal promises wealth and influence to a select group of owners. Rebecca recognizes that a competition built for them could leave the people who fill the stands with much less to believe in. She persuades the room by reminding her peers that they were once fans too. It is a fine character moment. It is also a very Ted Lasso solution: a person with power looks at other people more generously, then uses that power well. By the end of the third season, Rebecca even offers Richmond supporters a share of the club. Her change of heart matters, but she still chooses the terms on which they can participate. A real club has no writer to make the owner listen Manchester City has a different history and vastly different resources. City Football Group says it is majority owned through a company wholly owned by Sheikh Mansour, with Silver Lake holding a substantial minority stake. City's investment has helped build a club with global reach and success on the pitch. It has also made questions about financial reporting consequential for competitors who have to play under the same rules. On 29 September 2026, the Premier League published the findings of an independent commission . It upheld all substantive charges concerning breaches of financial rules from 2009/10 through 2017/18, as well as three of four charges concerning failure to cooperate with the league's investigation. The commission found that sham arrangements overstated revenue and understated costs by more than £900 million, giving the appearance that City complied with spending limits when it did not. City maintains its innocence and says it will appeal . A sanction has not yet been imposed. This is a question about accounts, oversight and competitive rules. It cannot tell us how much a City supporter loves the club, or dismiss the work of players and staff. It also cannot be resolved by asking whether the owner feels an emotional connection to football. The league has to establish what happened and enforce its rules through a process that can withstand challenge. Football's invisible decisions Ted Lasso makes club administration visible through Rebecca and Higgins. They have names and faces, so we can see when a decision hurts someone and when another decision begins to repair it. Real administration often consists of contracts, accounts and regulatory proceedings. It shapes what clubs can spend, who can compete and whether other clubs trust the result. The City process shows how difficult accountability can be after the fact. The league says its investigation began in December 2018; the commission hearing ended in December 2024, and its core findings were published in September 2026. City has the right to appeal and the question of sanction remains open. Whatever follows, those seasons cannot be played again. That delay matters to City's supporters as well as its rivals, all of whom have had to live with the unresolved case. Richmond's pub regulars remind us why any of this has stakes. A club is part of how people spend their weeks and remember their lives. City's fans have that relationship with their team too. Ownership can fund a stadium, recruit talent and take a club across the world, but those decisions do not give owners a greater claim to its meaning than the people who have stayed with it. The part television cannot settle Rebecca's speech is moving because it imagines someone powerful remembering what it felt like to have no power in the game. More owners could stand to remember that. But the scene ends when the owners agree. It has little reason to ask what happens when they do not, or when a decision is hidden in financial paperwork for years. That is why the City ruling belongs in this conversation without turning City into Ted Lasso 's villain. The commission's findings, City's appeal and the eventual sanction need to be judged on their own evidence. Richmond supplies a question worth bringing to that process: who pays for the choices made at the top of a club? The real answer has to be written into rules and enforced in time for the people outside the owners' room to trust them.

title: 9 Overlooked Platforming Gems Worth Revisiting
description: Rescue Rangers, Earthworm Jim, Jazz Jackrabbit, Dangerous Dave and more: nine retro platforming picks worth revisiting, with clear version notes.
body: A cardboard box is a surprisingly good weapon when you are a chipmunk. Pick it up, throw it at a mechanical dog, then duck beneath another while your partner decides whether to help or hurl you across the screen. Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers understood that a small set of good actions could carry an entire adventure. That is the appeal of this corner of platforming history. Mario and Sonic are obvious return visits, but the cartridges and early PC games around them held cartoon adaptations, odd mascots and action games with ideas worth borrowing. Some of these sold well. Aladdin and The Lion King are familiar names, hardly secret discoveries. The case here is for playing them again, alongside games that receive much less attention. These are nine picks across consoles and DOS, not a strict ranking. The list stretches from straightforward platformers to action games where jumping shares the controller with fighting. Versions matter: a familiar title on a different console can be a different game altogether. 1. Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers Version: NES. Best for: two-player mischief. Capcom makes being small the whole point. Boxes become ammunition and hiding places, while oversized furniture turns an ordinary room into a landscape. You can understand the basic moves almost immediately, then spend the rest of a stage discovering what else those moves permit. The original manual even explains how steel boxes can be stacked to reach higher platforms. Two-player play adds a useful amount of chaos. Carrying and throwing a partner can solve a problem or create one, depending on the mood of the person beside you. It gives cooperation a physical, slightly mischievous quality. The game is also perfectly enjoyable alone; having someone to blame for a bad landing is a bonus. 2. Mighty Morphin Power Rangers Version: the 1994 SNES game. Best for: a short burst of Saturday-morning action. This is the genre-borderline pick. Natsume's game is primarily a side-scrolling brawler, with climbing, jumping and platforming sections along its single-plane stages. What earns it a place is how neatly it stages the television fantasy. The early levels begin with your chosen Ranger in civilian clothes, then let you morph before the boss encounter. Later, the scale changes again for Megazord battles. The fighting is simple and the enemy designs repeat, so this is a modest recommendation rather than a lost masterpiece. Still, the transformation gives a familiar stage structure a little anticipation. If your memory is of a different Power Rangers cartridge, check the platform: the Genesis original is a fighting game, not this SNES adventure. SNES version details . 3. The Lion King Versions: SNES and Mega Drive/Genesis. Best for: animation and a challenge you may still resent. The opening has a confidence few film adaptations manage. Young Simba bounds through bright scenery, and his movement sells the character before the game needs much explanation. Growing into adult Simba changes the emphasis from a cub's pouncing and roaring toward more direct combat. Even in a short platformer, that change gives the journey a sense of development. Then there is the obstacle course accompanying I Just Can't Wait to Be King . Its monkeys, giraffes and timing demands make a cheerful scene feel considerably less cheerful. The difficulty is uneven, and attractive animation cannot excuse every awkward jump. Revisit it for the craft and the changing character, with realistic expectations about the frustration. This entry concerns the 16-bit games; the NES and handheld releases should not be treated as identical versions. SNES gameplay reference . 4. Aladdin Versions: Capcom's SNES game and Virgin's Mega Drive/Genesis game. Best for: comparing two interpretations of one film. There are two recommendations under this heading. Capcom's Aladdin puts its emphasis on movement, jumps and acrobatics. Apples can stun enemies before you bounce on them; the pleasure is in keeping the journey moving. Virgin's version gives Aladdin a sword as well as throwable apples, with animation that makes even a brief exchange with a guard entertaining to watch. Choose the SNES game if platforming is the main attraction. Choose the Genesis game if expressive characters and swordplay are what you remember. Better still, try both and notice how the same source material produces different rhythms. They are separate games, not a single port with altered colours. The Disney Classic Games Collection includes both 16-bit interpretations; it is an expanded package compared with the original 2019 collection. Capcom version background ; Genesis mechanics . 5. Shadow of the Ninja Version: NES, also known as Blue Shadow in Europe. Best for: a ninja adventure you can share. A second ninja changes the appeal immediately. Hayate and Kaede can fight through Natsume's action platformer together, with enemies and gaps demanding attention even when there are two of you. Hanging from platforms and choosing when to commit to an attack make movement part of the fighting, rather than a pause between encounters. The futuristic streets and machinery give the adventure a harsher atmosphere than the cartoon games here. Its difficulty asks both players to learn the route, and company does not make every jump forgiving. That is part of the satisfaction: clearing a troublesome section together feels earned. This entry is for the original NES game, called Kage in Japan and Blue Shadow in Europe; the later Shadow of the Ninja Reborn is a separate remake. Original game and cooperative play . 6. Earthworm Jim Versions: the original Mega Drive/Genesis and SNES games. Best for: strange sights and physical comedy. Jim's suit gives him a gun, but his own body is the better joke. He can use his worm head as a whip to strike enemies and catch hooks, turning a ridiculous character design into a useful platforming move. The animation carries that absurdity into the way he stands, moves and reacts. Even the opening's cow-launching gag makes the world feel happily unhinged. Shiny keeps interrupting the usual run-and-jump routine with different situations, including rocket races and the job of protecting Peter Puppy. Those detours give the game personality, although some are more frustrating than funny when you have to repeat them. Revisit it for its expressive action and willingness to be strange, rather than expecting every experiment to land. The 16-bit releases, later Special Edition and handheld adaptations are not all interchangeable. Original versions and gameplay . 7. Darkwing Duck Version: NES. Best for: careful jumps and a hero with more confidence than health. The gas gun is the obvious tool, but Darkwing's cape and ability to hang from ledges make the game more interesting than a simple march to the right. You can block certain incoming attacks, wait for an opening, then climb back into the action. It asks you to notice enemy placement and make room for a clean shot. Special gas adds further possibilities, including arrows that can help with traversal. It is a compact example of how a character's equipment can shape a platformer. Expect to learn troublesome sections rather than sail through on cartoon charm. If DuckTales is already on your replay list, this is a worthwhile companion with a sharper action emphasis. Controls and special weapons . 8. Jazz Jackrabbit Version: the original 1994 DOS game. Best for: fast movement with a gun in your hands. Jazz brings mascot-platformer energy to the PC: a green rabbit, a red bandana and enough speed to make you watch the next stretch of ground carefully. His gun changes the rhythm. You can clear threats while moving, but running too eagerly still puts you into trouble. The pleasure is in finding a route you can take at pace without losing control of the situation. Collecting ammunition lets you switch away from the basic blaster, with weapons such as bouncing projectiles and missiles that split into a V-shaped shot. The original on-disk manual explains the arsenal. This recommendation is for the first Jazz Jackrabbit , not its sequel. The Jazz Jackrabbit Collection groups the original episodes, additional CD episodes and Holiday Hare outings, making the scope of the release worth checking. 9. Dangerous Dave Version: the 1990 DOS game. Best for: a small challenge with no room for careless jumps. Find the trophy, then reach the exit. Dangerous Dave gives you a goal that fits in a sentence, but the route can make you think twice. Fire, awkward ledges and moving enemies turn a simple screen into a sequence you need to understand. A gun or jetpack can change your options, making the journey to a useful pickup part of the problem. It is plainer and less fluid than the big 16-bit productions in this list, and its unforgiving hazards can make a short attempt end abruptly. The appeal is how quickly it gets down to business. There is very little between starting the game and having a jump worth concentrating on. Here, “Dave” means the original DOS Dangerous Dave , rather than Dangerous Dave in the Haunted Mansion . John Romero's series history identifies the 1990 PC release; his level notes describe the trophies, weapons and jetpack routes. Where to start For an easy first decision, choose Rescue Rangers with a friend or Capcom's Aladdin for platforming. Try Earthworm Jim for strange comedy, Jazz Jackrabbit for speed, or Dangerous Dave for a compact DOS challenge. Pick Shadow of the Ninja when you want to learn a demanding route with someone beside you. The strongest reason to revisit these games is a specific action that still feels good: throwing the box, catching the ledge, landing the head whip. Get that right and an old game needs very little help to become interesting again.

title: 5 NES and Famicom Shooters Worth Taking Flight For
description: Sky Destroyer, Galaga, Xevious, Macross and Gradius: five NES and Famicom shooters worth revisiting for their flying, fighting and weapon choices.
body: A green plane, a blue ocean and enemy fighters growing larger as they approach. Sky Destroyer creates the feeling of flying somewhere with very little scenery. The aircraft stays in view, the horizon gives you a direction, and a threat can arrive from the sky or the water below. That image is one reason to return to an old shooter. A good mechanic is another. Macross lets a fighter grow arms and legs to change how it handles a battle. Gradius turns an unremarkable little gun into an arsenal you have chosen and built. Galaga makes losing a ship the beginning of a dangerous rescue opportunity. These are five favourites worth revisiting, ranked by how much their distinctive ideas give me reason to recommend them today. The list includes aircraft and spacecraft, as well as Japan-only Famicom releases. Each entry concerns the original home version, rather than assuming an arcade game or later adaptation with the same name plays identically. 5. Sky Destroyer Version: Famicom, Japan-only. Style: behind-the-plane aerial combat. The viewpoint is its best idea. Looking past your own aircraft toward the horizon gives enemy approaches a sense of distance that a flat formation cannot provide. Machine-gun fire handles aerial threats, while torpedoes let you attack targets at sea. You have a small set of controls, but two different parts of the scene to watch. Aircraft, weapons and objectives . The cycle of changing light helps sell the illusion of a sortie. Reaching a fortified island gives that flight a destination; taking it out is more satisfying than simply seeing another wave appear. Those details are modest, yet they give the game a recognisable atmosphere. Its limits are equally clear. The encounters repeat, and the action offers less variety than the games above it. Treat it as a short return visit, rather than expecting an elaborate campaign. If your memory is of a plane suspended over an endless ocean, the opening should bring it back quickly. The 1985 Famicom release is the version covered here. 4. Galaga: Demons of Death Version: NES; Galaga on Famicom. Style: fixed-screen space shooting. Moving left and right beneath a formation sounds restrictive until the formation starts coming apart. Enemies dive toward you, changing the safe space at the bottom of the screen. Chasing the next target is tempting, but watching the direction of an approaching attack is often more useful. The controls stay simple while your reading of the screen improves. The capture mechanic gives that small battlefield another layer. Allow a fighter to be taken, then successfully rescue it, and you can form a dual fighter with greater firepower. You are risking a ship to improve your position. The NES manual explains how the rescue works. That gamble is the main reason I would choose Galaga over a more basic formation shooter. It introduces a decision that can change the feel of the run without adding a menu or complicated controls. The scenery hardly changes, so the satisfaction has to come from better judgement, cleaner shooting and a higher score. For a few concentrated minutes of play, that remains a very good bargain. 3. Xevious Version: NES/Famicom. Style: vertically scrolling air-and-ground combat. A gun fires forward at enemies in the air. A targeting reticle marks where your bombs will hit the ground. That separation is the whole appeal of Xevious : lining up a ground installation can put your aircraft in a bad position for an aerial attack. A safe route and a profitable bombing run are not always the same route. The scrolling landscape gives those decisions a setting. Ground defences pass beneath you while airborne enemies interrupt your plan, and the large floating fortress adds a threat with more presence than a small formation. Nintendo's description of the NES game identifies the two kinds of attack. The presentation is restrained, and the fixed arsenal will disappoint anyone looking for a stream of spectacular upgrades. Give it a little time to establish its rhythm, though, and the two-layer combat becomes rewarding. You improve by placing the ship better and recognising which threat needs attention first. It is a useful step up from Galaga if you want a moving world and more freedom without learning a lengthy equipment system. 2. The Super Dimension Fortress Macross Version: Famicom, Japan-only. Style: horizontal space shooting with a transforming fighter. The Valkyrie can be a fighter, the halfway GERWALK form, or a humanoid Battroid. Changing form affects speed and firing capabilities, so the transformation has a purpose beyond looking impressive. Fighter mode lets you move quickly; Battroid's ability to fire behind itself changes how you deal with an enemy that has slipped past. The machine's appearance tells you something useful about what it can do. The mission structure supports that fantasy. You fight through space, approach a large enemy warship, then enter its interior to destroy the reactor. That progression makes each sortie feel like an assault on a target, with the final approach asking you to handle a different kind of space. Forms and mission stages . Repetition eventually catches up with it, and the early graphics cannot disguise how often the same basic mission returns. Still, the transformations make familiar combat more engaging. Learning when to change the craft feels different from merely collecting a stronger gun. This is Namco's 1985 Famicom game, a specific recommendation within a much larger family of Macross adaptations. 1. Gradius Version: NES/Famicom. Style: horizontal space shooting with selectable upgrades. Every red capsule moves the highlight along the power meter. You decide when to activate it: take an improvement now, or keep collecting toward something else. That is a small but powerful change to the usual pickup system. Building the ship becomes a succession of choices made while you are still dodging enemies. The weapons make those choices visible. Missiles deal with targets below you, a laser improves your forward attack, and Options follow the ship and copy its firepower. Getting those companions into position turns a narrow stream of shots into something much more capable. You can feel the difference between the fighter you started with and the formation you have assembled. Konami's NES manual details the upgrades. Losing the equipment is painful, especially when you have grown accustomed to clearing threats quickly. Recovery can feel punishing. Yet that also gives a good run its tension: you are protecting a machine you helped build. Of these five games, Gradius offers the strongest combination of immediate shooting and decisions worth thinking about between attempts. The next capsule is rarely just another object to collect. Where to begin Choose Sky Destroyer for the ocean view, Galaga for formation reading, or Xevious for the challenge of watching two layers of combat. Macross is the pick if you want to transform the machine itself. Start with Gradius if the memory that brought you here was a small spaceship gradually gaining missiles, lasers and companions. Each asks you to notice something different: an approach from the horizon, a formation breaking, a ground target passing beneath you, a reason to transform, or an upgrade worth waiting for. Learning to see those opportunities is what makes another short flight worthwhile.

title: From DuckTales to The Punisher: 4 Retro Collections Worth Playing
description: TMNT, Marvel vs. Capcom, Disney and SNK: four retro game collections worth playing, with standout games and the version differences that matter.
body: Scrooge McDuck can still make a pogo stick out of a walking cane. Wolverine can still fill half a screen with claws. Four turtles can still turn a street full of disposable enemies into a very good evening. The appeal of returning to these games begins with an action you remember, then grows when the rest of the game proves worth remembering too. A retro collection needs to make that return easy. The right versions, useful controls and a sensible way to save matter more than a huge number on the box. Artwork and development notes can deepen the experience, especially when they help explain why an old game made the choices it did. But there should also be something inside that you want to keep playing after the museum closes. These four collections offer different routes back: cooperative arcade action, superhero fighting, cartoon platformers and a tour of SNK before the Neo Geo. They are four recommendations, rather than a ranking of interchangeable packages. Each earns its place for a different reason, and each has a few details worth checking before you buy. 1. Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection Start with: Turtles in Time, The Hyperstone Heist and The Manhattan Project. The turtles are unusually well suited to a collection. Their games share enough characters and ideas to feel like one shelf of adventures, yet change substantially as you move between arcade cabinets, Nintendo consoles, the Genesis and Game Boy. A sewer, a skateboard and a familiar villain can become very different things depending on the hardware. The Cowabunga Collection gathers 13 games , including both the arcade and SNES versions of Turtles in Time . Having them together makes comparison part of the fun. You can see how a home adaptation reshapes a game, rather than treating every console release as the same experience with fewer colours. The strongest reason to start here is the brawling. Turtles in Time keeps changing the backdrop while letting you settle into the satisfying business of clearing a screen. The Hyperstone Heist gives Genesis players their own take on that rhythm, while the NES Manhattan Project squeezes an energetic adventure out of simpler hardware. They work particularly well when another player joins the argument over which turtle to choose. The package also makes room for the less obvious attraction, Radical Rescue . That Game Boy adventure gives different turtles abilities that open routes through its map. It is a useful reminder that the licence supported more than one kind of action game. Digital Eclipse treats the surrounding material with care. Restored manuals, development artwork, music and strategy guides sit alongside save and rewind features. The guides even offer help with the original NES game's notorious underwater section. Those additions give younger players a chance to understand the games without inheriting every frustration that came with them. The catch: thirteen titles do not mean thirteen equally strong games. The fighting games and early handheld outings have different appeals from the headline brawlers, and online play is limited to selected titles. Buy it for the adventures you want to play, then let the rest become discoveries. 2. Marvel vs. Capcom Fighting Collection: Arcade Classics Start with: Marvel vs. Capcom 2, X-Men vs. Street Fighter and The Punisher. Few collections announce themselves quite like this one. Superheroes leap far above the ground, special attacks spill across the screen, and the roster treats comic-book absurdity as a design brief. The pleasure is partly in the fighting and partly in seeing how enthusiastically Capcom translates these characters into animation. The seven-game lineup follows that partnership from X-Men: Children of the Atom and Marvel Super Heroes through X-Men vs. Street Fighter , Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter , Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes and Marvel vs. Capcom 2: New Age of Heroes . The seventh game takes a different route: The Punisher is a side-scrolling beat 'em up. Marvel vs. Capcom 2 is the obvious centrepiece. Choosing a team gives even a casual match its own little fantasy: favourite characters, unlikely combinations and the possibility that someone dismissed as a novelty will become your favourite fighter. Learning what those teams can actually do is a much larger project. The roster's appeal survives that gap between picking characters and mastering them. X-Men vs. Street Fighter is a rewarding earlier stop. Its pairings feel immediately legible if you grew up with either franchise, and swapping partners gives familiar one-on-one fighting a different rhythm. Playing the series in sequence lets you watch the crossover idea expand. Then there is The Punisher . It is reason enough for arcade-brawler fans to pay attention, even if competitive fighting leaves them cold. Frank Castle and Nick Fury take Capcom's street-fighting formula through a nastier comic-book world, with weapons and environmental destruction adding to the spectacle. Its presence gives the package a welcome change of pace. Training options, galleries and rollback online play help these games find a place beyond a nostalgic afternoon. The collection is available for Switch, PS4, Xbox One and Steam; console compatibility with newer hardware depends on the version you buy. The catch: six of the seven games are fighters. If The Punisher is your only attraction, wait for a price you can justify for that game alone. There is plenty here for anyone interested in learning the others, but a large roster does not make a demanding fighter automatically approachable. 3. The Disney Afternoon Collection Start with: DuckTales, Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers and Darkwing Duck. Add Goof Troop on the newer Nintendo edition. There is a satisfying economy to Capcom's Disney games. Scrooge's cane, the chipmunks' throwable boxes and Darkwing's gas gun give each character an immediately useful identity. Their television personalities survive through movement and tools, without needing long conversations to establish who they are. The original collection contains six NES games: DuckTales , DuckTales 2 , Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers , Rescue Rangers 2 , TaleSpin and Darkwing Duck . The 2026 Switch and Switch 2 edition adds the SNES games Goof Troop and Bonkers , bringing its lineup to eight. Check the edition carefully: those additions are exclusive to the newer Nintendo release. DuckTales remains the most inviting starting point. The pogo jump turns enemies into stepping stones, and the levels give you reasons to look around rather than hurry straight to the exit. DuckTales 2 offers a less famous continuation with new uses for the cane. Together they make a compact case for character-driven platforming. Rescue Rangers shifts the pleasure towards cooperation. Throwing a box is simple; deciding whether to throw your partner is a matter of character. Both games are enjoyable alone, but another player brings the sort of mild mischief that a perfectly orderly cooperative game can miss. Darkwing Duck supplies the sharper action challenge. Its shooting, hanging and special weapons reward more deliberate movement. For players who like Capcom's NES action games, it is a natural companion to the more exploratory DuckTales . On the newer edition, Goof Troop adds a different kind of partnership. Its overhead puzzles turn cooperation into a problem of positioning and timing. That change of genre helps the Nintendo package feel broader, while keeping its cartoon charm. Rewind and saves throughout the collection also make a return visit much less dependent on spare lives or remembering passwords. The catch: the weaker games remain weaker games. TaleSpin has awkward shooting and a slow plane; Bonkers has attractive animation without the same quality of level design. A detailed review of the newer edition makes the same distinction. The stronger platformers and Goof Troop carry the recommendation. Also, these are the original games: DuckTales Remastered is a separate release. 4. SNK 40th Anniversary Collection Start with: Crystalis, the arcade Ikari Warriors and Psycho Soldier. Try Prehistoric Isle for dinosaur-powered arcade nonsense. SNK's name tends to bring Metal Slug and The King of Fighters to mind. This collection looks further back, at the company's work before the Neo Geo. Its appeal is finding the experiments that preceded the familiar identity: tanks, soldiers, strange platformers and shooters with ideas that had not yet settled into a house style. The strongest discovery is Crystalis . This NES action RPG gives the collection an adventure substantial enough to occupy more than a short arcade session. Its sword combat, exploration and progression make it a particularly good choice for anyone who enjoys the early Zelda games. Nintendo World Report and the much more sceptical GameCritics review both identify it as the standout. The arcade games reward a more exploratory approach. Ikari Warriors lets you see why the overhead soldier-and-vehicle format became recognisable. Psycho Soldier brings cooperative shooting to a colourful platform-action framework. Prehistoric Isle in 1930 sends a plane into a world of dinosaurs, a premise whose appeal needs very little historical explanation. Some games include their NES adaptations as well as the arcade originals. That makes the collection especially interesting as a study of compromises. It also makes choosing the right version important. The arcade Ikari Warriors and its NES port have very different reputations; Athena is another game where the format changes the recommendation substantially. The surrounding features are unusually useful. Rewind helps tame coin-hungry difficulty, and the watch mode lets you study a recorded playthrough before taking control. The museum provides artwork, promotional material and background that can turn an unfamiliar title into something worth investigating. The catch: this is the least consistently enjoyable lineup of the four. Historical interest does a fair amount of the work. SNK's official Steam roster lists 24 games; console editions also include Iron Tank , and Xbox adds Baseball Stars . Check your platform's contents, and do not buy it expecting the Neo Geo favourites. Which collection should you choose? For cooperative brawling, start with Cowabunga . For comic-book spectacle and a fighter you can keep learning, choose Marvel vs. Capcom . Disney is the most reliable route to colourful platforming, especially if the newer edition's Goof Troop is an option. SNK suits a more curious mood, with Crystalis giving its scattered discoveries a strong centre. The best return visits begin with something small: a well-timed throw, a pogo jump, a partner tagging into a fight. These collections make those actions easy to find again. The good ones can still turn a quick look into an evening.

title: 15 of the Best VR Games Ever Made
description: From Half-Life: Alyx to Astro Bot and Arkham Shadow, 15 landmark VR games worth celebrating as Sony's reported patent transfers raise new questions.
body: Leaning around a doorway should be a small action. In a good VR game, it can become the whole encounter: a glimpse of an enemy, a hand searching for ammunition, the decision to pull back before something notices you. That change in scale is what the medium does best. Familiar actions acquire weight because your body has to take part in them. The recent Sony and Meta headlines make this a timely moment to revisit that achievement. Road to VR's 7 October 2026 report , drawing on ZDNet Korea's reporting, describes 43 recorded US patent transfers between June and September, within a wider agreement covering XR patents. That is a reported patent transaction, not a confirmed sale of Sony's entire VR business or an announcement that PSVR2 has ended. Both companies had yet to comment in that report. The uncertainty still raises a useful question: which games deserve to outlast the hardware arguments? These fifteen are an editorial selection of the best VR games, ranked for how well they use the medium, the strength of their underlying design and their lasting appeal. The list includes dedicated VR games and substantial VR modes, across generations. It is not a ranking of headset specifications or an average of review scores. Platform notes identify the relevant VR editions, not every possible hardware configuration. An original PSVR game does not automatically work on PSVR2; Sony's compatibility guidance explicitly separates the libraries. Check the linked edition before buying. Research and version notes were checked on 14 October 2026. 1. Half-Life: Alyx VR edition: SteamVR. The benchmark for a sustained VR campaign. The gravity gloves are a clever answer to an everyday problem: an object you want is slightly too far away. Flicking it towards your hand is convenient, expressive and enjoyable often enough to become a habit. Alyx builds that kind of thoughtfulness into an entire adventure. Combat gains tension from the work between shots. Looking for ammunition, handling a reload and making use of cover become decisions made with your hands and posture. Meanwhile, drawers and shelves give exploration a useful physical texture. You examine a place by doing something in it. Valve balances those details with strong pacing, recognisable Half-Life humour and carefully staged fear. Its official overview places the story between the first two main games. The achievement is how comfortably that full adventure accommodates interaction at arm's length. It remains the first recommendation for someone who wants to see what a major campaign can gain from VR. 2. Astro Bot Rescue Mission VR edition: original PSVR, with PS Camera and DualShock 4. Rescue Mission makes your position in the world part of its platforming. Astro has somewhere to go, but you have somewhere to look. Leaning, peering around scenery and noticing a tiny robot tucked into an unlikely corner become pleasures alongside the jumps. The game keeps finding ways to let the player participate without taking the controller away from the little hero. The result is an adventure with an unusually warm relationship between scale and character. Astro feels small, the scenery feels substantial, and helping him feels personal. The original game's hardware requirements matter here. This is the 2018 VR adventure, not the later flat-screen Astro Bot , and its PSVR edition is not playable through PSVR2. That separation is also an argument for preserving it. One of Sony's most inventive uses of VR should remain easy to experience as hardware changes. 3. Beat Saber VR editions: Meta Quest, SteamVR, PSVR and PSVR2. Coloured blocks arrive, arrows tell you where to cut, and your arms learn the song. Beat Saber makes the rules clear enough to grasp immediately, then gives their execution enough room for years of improvement. The satisfaction comes from the whole motion: preparation, swing and the cut landing with the music. A difficult pattern gradually becomes a sequence you can recognise and perform. It is a strong example of a game where physical repetition is the pleasure, rather than a cumbersome substitute for a button press. Its place on this list also rests on accessibility. You do not need to understand a fictional world before you understand what is fun. Platform support has changed, though: the official FAQ says new PlayStation updates ended in June 2025 and PlayStation multiplayer ended in February 2026. Existing single-player content remains playable. Quest and Steam are the relevant editions for continuing content support. 4. Resident Evil 4 VR Mode Selected edition: the PS5 remake's PSVR2 mode. The village attack is a very different proposition when a chainsaw approaches at your own apparent height. Resident Evil 4 already understands pressure, crowd management and the need to keep moving. Its VR mode brings those demands closer without losing the larger adventure that makes the game special. Handling weapons, aiming with both hands and meeting an attack with a knife make familiar combat newly absorbing. The spectacle becomes more immediate, but the decision-making remains important. Being inside Leon's view does not remove the need to know when a fight is getting out of hand. Capcom's VR development interview confirms that the PSVR2 mode covers the remake's main campaign and is an additional download for owners of the PS5 game. Armature's Quest adaptation of the 2005 original is a separate, excellent interpretation. They should not be confused at the checkout. 5. Gran Turismo 7 VR edition: PS5 with PSVR2. Racing makes a persuasive case for VR without needing to reinvent its controls. You are already meant to be sitting inside a machine. Giving that cockpit depth changes the relationship between your car, the corner ahead and the rival drawing alongside. The gain is especially clear in ordinary racing decisions. You can look towards the exit of a bend, judge another car's position and glance at the interior without switching between fixed camera views. A steering wheel can deepen the effect, but it is not required to understand it. The PSVR2 update is included with the PS5 game at no additional charge. GT7 earns its position because VR serves a substantial racing game with reasons to return beyond the novelty of a first lap. The menus and occasional non-VR elements also make it worth understanding the mode's scope before expecting every moment to happen inside the cockpit. 6. SUPERHOT VR VR editions: Quest, SteamVR and original PSVR. Holding still gives you time to think. Moving commits you to the consequences. That relationship turns a room of red enemies into a problem you solve with your body: lean away from a shot, reach for a weapon, throw something across the space and follow the opening it creates. The sparse visuals help enormously. Threats are readable, objects are distinct, and very little scenery competes with the action. A successful sequence can feel choreographed even when it began as a desperate improvisation. The developer's FAQ makes an important distinction: SUPERHOT VR is a separate game with its own levels and mechanics, rather than a headset toggle for the flat-screen original. Its compactness is part of the appeal. It can demonstrate a very specific use of VR in minutes, then keep asking you to perform it better. 7. Batman: Arkham Shadow VR edition: Meta Quest 3 and Quest 3S. Turning Arkham combat into first-person action could easily have reduced Batman to a pair of swinging fists. Arkham Shadow keeps more of the identity intact: reading threats, using gadgets, moving through dangerous spaces and making a group of enemies manageable through controlled aggression. The physical actions give that fantasy a useful new texture. A punch belongs to your arm; a stealth encounter puts a target within reach. At the same time, the campaign retains investigation and atmosphere, giving Batman things to do between fights. The official game page identifies this as a full-length Arkham entry for Quest 3 and 3S. Its Best VR/AR win at The Game Awards 2024 is useful recognition, but the stronger recommendation is the design itself. It makes a familiar superhero game work from an unfamiliar viewpoint. 8. Asgard's Wrath 2 VR edition: Meta Quest standalone. An expansive RPG is a different test of VR from a perfect ten-minute encounter. It needs travel, character growth, combat and puzzles to remain worthwhile after the first impressive vista. Asgard's Wrath 2 takes on that larger problem with unusual confidence. Its changes in scale are especially effective. Fighting from a mortal's perspective and manipulating a puzzle at godly scale give the adventure different kinds of physical involvement. Companions and evolving equipment then help turn those moments into an ongoing journey. The official player's guide details its RPG systems and exploration. The attraction is the commitment to an extended adventure on standalone hardware. Choose it when you want a game to settle into over many sessions, rather than something to demonstrate to a friend before passing the headset over. 9. Resident Evil 7: Biohazard Selected edition: the PS4 game's original PSVR mode. The Baker house is effective because so much of it is horribly ordinary. A hallway, a table and a doorway can carry the dread before anything monstrous arrives. VR makes their dimensions feel harder to dismiss. Resident Evil 7 uses that proximity to support a full survival-horror campaign. It does not need elaborate hand interactions to make a room threatening. Looking towards a sound, hesitating before entering a space and checking what is behind you are already powerful actions. The official PSVR edition belongs to the older headset library. The PS5 flat-screen release is not a PSVR2 upgrade. Its presence here reflects the strength of that original VR experience, including its limitations, rather than an assumption that every modern Resident Evil 7 purchase includes the same mode. 10. The Walking Dead: Saints & Sinners VR editions include SteamVR, Quest and PlayStation VR releases; choose the version for your headset. Survival becomes more persuasive when the equipment has to be handled. Reaching for a weapon while a walker closes the distance changes a familiar inventory decision into an immediate task. The fighting has a physical quality that suits its desperate world. The original Saints & Sinners also gives you reasons to think beyond the next enemy. Scavenging, limited resources and encounters with the living make each trip into New Orleans a calculation. You are deciding what a risk is worth, then carrying out the decision at close range. That connection between preparation and action is why the game belongs here. VR contributes to the systems rather than merely putting zombies nearer your face. This recommendation is for the first game, not the separately sold Chapter 2: Retribution . 11. Moss: Book II VR editions: PSVR/PSVR2, Quest, SteamVR and Pico. Quill gives VR a protagonist you can care about without pretending to be her. You guide the mouse through the adventure while also reaching into her world to help. That partnership makes the viewpoint emotionally useful. Looking closely at a scene can reveal a route or a detail, and interacting with the environment gives the miniature world a pleasing solidity. The sequel adds tools and possibilities while preserving the appeal of watching a small, expressive hero tackle a large problem. Polyarc's Book II page confirms its VR platforms and 2022 Best VR/AR award. Start with the first Moss if you want Quill's story in order. Book II takes the place here as the richer continuation, but both demonstrate how well VR can serve an adventure observed from the outside. 12. Walkabout Mini Golf VR editions include Quest, PC VR, PSVR2 and Pico. There is a particular pleasure in lining up a putt, choosing how hard to hit it and watching the ball obey a plan that was nearly good enough. Walkabout builds its appeal around that ordinary, repeatable satisfaction. The courses then give the act of putting somewhere memorable to happen. Their layouts encourage you to examine the scenery, find another angle and occasionally wonder whether a ridiculous bank shot might work. Searching for hidden balls supplies a second reason to linger. Mighty Coconut's course overview and platform guide explain the available editions and cross-platform play. In company, the game becomes a place to spend time as well as something to win. It deserves a place among the grand adventures because it understands a smaller ambition so completely. 13. Lone Echo VR edition: Meta's Rift/PC VR release; not a native Quest standalone game. Reaching for a surface and pushing away gives zero-gravity movement a satisfying logic. Your hands explain the environment: how to stop, how to turn, how to travel without a floor doing the work. Lone Echo combines that movement with the relationship between Jack and Liv aboard a mining facility near Saturn. Being beside another character, helping with practical tasks and inhabiting the same space make the science-fiction story more immediate. The original PC VR listing is an important version distinction for Quest owners. The game's place here rests on its strong marriage of movement and companionship. Its sequel is another worthwhile stop, but the first establishes why reaching through a virtual space can feel so natural. 14. Pistol Whip VR editions: Quest, SteamVR and PlayStation VR releases, including PSVR2. Pistol Whip gives a shooting gallery a beat, then asks your body to keep up. A shot, a dodge and a close-range strike become parts of the same performance. The appeal is how quickly they can begin to feel connected. Its visual scenes are deliberately stylised, helping the action remain readable while the music supplies momentum. Chasing a better run can mean learning where threats appear, tightening your timing or choosing a different challenge. Familiarity improves the fantasy of moving cleanly through a dangerous scene. The official Steam description outlines that blend of rhythm and film-inspired gunplay. It sits alongside Beat Saber because it offers a different physical conversation with music: shooting and evasion instead of cutting patterns. 15. No Man's Sky VR editions include SteamVR and PlayStation VR/PSVR2. Stepping out of a ship gives No Man's Sky a different sense of scale. The cockpit you occupied a moment ago becomes a machine beside you, and the landscape extends beyond the edge of a monitor. Exploration gains a useful pause: a reason to stand still before deciding where to go. It is a less tightly designed VR showcase than Alyx or SUPERHOT . The attraction is the freedom to make a longer journey through its existing universe: flying, gathering, building and finding somewhere you want to remain. Hello Games' Fractal update notes document the PSVR2 implementation. Performance and presentation depend on your hardware and settings, so expectations matter. Its place on this list comes from scale and possibility. Few games offer quite the same feeling of owning a little ship in a very large space. A few more worth making room for Tetris Effect: Connected and Rez Infinite deserve attention for turning sound and imagery into spaces you can occupy. Red Matter 2 is a strong choice for tactile puzzles and a carefully realised science-fiction atmosphere. Eleven Table Tennis makes another persuasive case for keeping a familiar sport's physical actions intact. Blade & Sorcery suits players who want to experiment with the possibilities of physical combat. Fifteen places cannot cover every useful route into VR. These omissions are reasons to keep exploring, especially once you know whether you prefer rhythm, careful puzzles, extended campaigns or a world to inhabit. The games are worth keeping within reach If you want a first step, choose Beat Saber or Walkabout . For a major campaign, start with Alyx , Arkham Shadow or Asgard's Wrath 2 , depending on your hardware. For Sony's strongest demonstrations, Gran Turismo 7 and the PSVR2 Resident Evil 4 mode make an immediate case; Astro Bot Rescue Mission remains a compelling reason to preserve the older headset's library. The patent reports invite questions about what Sony intends to build next. The games leave a more practical question: how easily will people be able to experience what has already been built? A catalogue spread across incompatible headsets can be difficult to revisit even when its best ideas remain fresh. There is still something remarkable about finding yourself beside Quill, inside a racing car or holding a putter over an improbable little course. Whatever the next hardware cycle brings, those are experiences worth keeping within reach.

title: Grand Theft Auto: The American Dream Has a Wanted Level
description: How GTA evolved from overhead chaos to criminal empires: every era, its stories, music and satire, and what GTA VI could change.
body: From stolen hatchbacks to criminal empires, how GTA changed its cities, its stories and its idea of freedom, and what GTA VI needs to get right. There is a moment in Grand Theft Auto when the mission stops mattering. You were supposed to collect somebody. Then a better car went past. Then the radio played something you liked. Then the police arrived, an unfortunate misunderstanding involving several pedestrians having occurred, and now you are reversing a burning ambulance up a motorway exit. Your contact can wait. He has been standing in the same place since Tuesday. Almost thirty years into the series, that diversion remains GTA's most persuasive sales pitch. Rockstar can write the betrayal, hire the actor and choreograph the helicopter crash. It still has to compete with whatever happens when you take the wrong turn. GTA VI is currently scheduled for 19 November 2026 , on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Rockstar's launch trailer arrived on 15 October. The return to Vice City is close enough to require actual calendar management, rather than another theory about the moon. But what, exactly, are we waiting to return to? For some players, GTA is the neon of Vice City. For others, it is a bicycle outside the Johnson house, a boat arriving in Liberty City, or three men arguing their way through a robbery. A growing part of its audience knows Los Santos primarily as somewhere to meet friends, run businesses and be murdered by equipment that appears to have escaped from a defence contractor's cocaine drawer. These games share a name and a remarkably durable appetite for stealing cars. Their ambitions have changed considerably. They have offered the fantasy of becoming powerful, asked whether power fixes anything, and eventually built an online economy that can make criminal prosperity feel suspiciously like maintaining a second job. To understand what VI might become, it helps to follow how that happened. The story starts in Scotland, well before anyone needed to count the hair on a trailer character's arm. Spoiler note: this article discusses premises, themes and several mid-story developments across the released games. It avoids explaining their final choices and endings. GTA VI discussion uses public material available by 16 October 2026. 1. Before the empire: GTA discovers that the detour is the game Grand Theft Auto, 1997 The original GTA arrived in a period when games were enthusiastically learning to look expensive. PlayStation was selling the promise of three-dimensional worlds; here was a top-down game in which your criminal ambitions were represented by a small person you could lose beneath the scenery. DMA Design's project had begun as Race 'n' Chase . Its development was messy, and the eventual formula emerged through iteration rather than a single immaculate design revelation. In a later interview, developer Gary Penn recalled instability, awful vehicle handling and a police-behaviour bug that made officers aggressively ram the player. He remembered that aggression helping the game become entertaining. It is a valuable recollection, with the uncertainty he attached to it intact: one developer's account of a breakthrough, rather than proof that the entire franchise happened by accident. The result let you move between vehicles, crimes and jobs across early versions of Liberty City, San Andreas and Vice City . Those names preceded their famous later incarnations. Narrative arrived in small messages and instructions; the real continuity was the money you earned and the trouble you accumulated. That abstraction mattered. Early GTA treated the city as something to interfere with. Missions gave you reasons to travel, but stealing a different vehicle could change the texture of the next minute. You could understand the place through what it allowed, and through the speed at which it became annoyed with you. It also established the radio. Much of the first game's music was created in-house by Colin Anderson, Craig Conner and Grant Middleton, rather than assembled from the licensed hits that would later become a series trademark. Even here, a car was both transport and a little room with music in it. GTA had found a way to make travelling entertaining before it could afford to make travelling beautiful. Its humour was less discriminating. The notorious bonus for running down a procession of Hare Krishnas belongs to this history too. Some of the early transgression is clever interaction; some is simply a game noticing that it can be offensive and getting rather pleased with itself. Those impulses would remain difficult to separate. The surrounding panic arrived astonishingly early. In May 1997, before the game's release, GTA was being discussed in the House of Lords. Lord Campbell of Croy raised concerns about a game involving theft and police pursuits. The institution was taking the threat seriously while the developers were still trying to make the cars behave. That mismatch became part of GTA's public identity. Adults arguing that a game was dangerous gave it an aura no advertising department could buy quite as convincingly. Yet outrage alone does not explain its endurance. Plenty of offensive games have disappeared without requiring an international countdown for their sequels. GTA had a repeatable pleasure beneath the scandal: a small decision could produce a large mess. London 1969 and London 1961, 1999 The two London mission packs are often treated as a geographical footnote. They deserve better. They showed, early, that changing a GTA's time and place could change its personality even when its underlying actions stayed familiar. London 1969 moved the formula into a British period-crime setting: left-hand traffic, different slang, vehicles and a soundtrack that helped establish the era. The smaller London 1961 followed as a free PC expansion. This was the seed of an approach Vice City would make famous. A setting could determine the jokes, the musical references and the sort of criminal fantasy being offered. You could steal a car in several games; the question was what stealing that car made you feel you were starring in. The London packs also complicate the claim that GTA has always been exclusively about America. It became overwhelmingly associated with America. For a brief period it was perfectly happy to send you down a British street, where organised crime could be conducted in the vicinity of a reasonably priced sandwich. GTA 2, 1999: somebody remembers who you annoyed GTA 2 kept the overhead view but moved into the deliberately strange, retrofuturistic Anywhere City . It also made gang relationships central. Work for one faction, damage another, and watch your standing change. Hostile territory could become a practical problem rather than a different colour on the map. Here was an early attempt to give freedom consequences beyond the police chase. The city had competing interests. Your access to work depended on how you positioned yourself among them. Its premise remained broader and less intimate than the character dramas to come. Claude Speed was not asking players to spend fifty hours processing the emotional history of a tracksuit. The gangs were extravagant types, with the Zaibatsu corporation making the overlap between criminal and corporate power especially unsubtle. At launch, however, refinement could look like repetition. GameSpot's contemporary review enjoyed the game while stressing how much of it remained familiar. That is useful perspective. GTA was not born as an unstoppable sequence of unanimously recognised masterpieces. The early games were finding their limits, too. One of their most interesting ideas would later become oddly peripheral: working relationships that change the way the city receives you. GTA VI could learn as much from that respect meter as from another decade of visual improvements. 2. GTA III: suddenly, the city has a horizon GTA III arrived on PlayStation 2 in October 2001. Putting the series into 3D changed the player's relationship with almost everything. The road now ran away from you. A building could conceal an escape route. A hill could reveal the next district. Driving towards a bridge felt different from moving a small car towards a line on a map. You occupied the city from inside the traffic. The breakthrough was the combination: driving, on-foot movement, gunfights, ambient pedestrians, police escalation and a crime story all operating in one explorable place. GTA III did not invent open worlds. It made this particular mixture feel like something an enormous number of people had been waiting to play. Its launch reviews recognised that immediately, even while acknowledging awkward controls and other rough edges. Claude, betrayed during a robbery, works through Liberty City's criminal networks. He barely needs a personality for the structure to function. Other people supply the threats, plans and self-importance; he supplies the labour. It is an arrangement familiar to anyone who has attended a meeting where somebody says, “We should really own this.” The mob-film influences gave the game an accessible dramatic language. You knew roughly what kind of room you were entering when a crime boss called. The city supplied the atmosphere: industrial grime, rain, commercial clutter and an impression that almost everybody was making a living at somebody else's expense. Its side activities helped loosen the boundaries of the fantasy. A taxi, ambulance or police vehicle could become the starting point for another sort of play. You might be the least trustworthy emergency worker in the borough, but the city still had a vacancy. Then there was Chatterbox . Radio turned the journeys between missions into encounters with people you never met. Commercials, callers and presenters suggested a society that continued being ridiculous while Claude was elsewhere. It was world-building that did not require the player to stop, read a document and demonstrate sufficient interest in the lore. GTA III's release environment also demands care. It launched weeks after the September 11 attacks, with Rockstar's New York operation directly affected. Later, the studio explained that it made limited changes, including alterations to packaging and some content. Its own retrospective pushed back against the mythology of a wholesale, last-minute rebuilding of the game. The historical distinction matters. A game developed before the attacks entered a profoundly different public atmosphere after them. That does not make every bridge, damaged car or police encounter an intentional response to the event. GTA III nevertheless established the series' defining tension. Liberty City appeared open to improvisation, while its story required a particular sequence of jobs. The player could discover a hundred ways to make trouble between missions, then encounter a mission that preferred one approved kind of trouble. For the moment, the city was extraordinary enough to make that bargain easy. 3. Vice City: ambition gets a swimming pool One year later, Vice City returned with an argument for style. Its 1986 setting brought pastel suits, beachside hotels, cocaine fortunes and the combined gravitational pull of Scarface and Miami Vice . Tommy Vercetti, voiced by Ray Liotta, arrives after a prison sentence and immediately loses his employer's money in a drug deal gone wrong. He spends the game recovering his position, discovering the city's opportunities and becoming considerably more difficult to manage. Giving the lead a voice changed the transaction. Claude received everybody else's personality. Tommy pushed back. He could be impatient, sarcastic and furious, allowing a scene to become a contest rather than a briefing delivered to a leather jacket. The property system gave his ascent a physical shape. Businesses generated work and eventually income. The city could gradually become a collection of things you owned. Buying a building was satisfying because it made the fantasy legible: you had started as somebody being shouted at over a telephone, and now other people were doing the worrying. This was GTA's American dream at its most seductive. Yes, the route involved murder. But look at the house. Vice City's critique of greed and its pleasure in acquisition continually fed each other. The game mocked status while furnishing an excellent selection of status symbols. It understood the attraction of the thing it was ridiculing, which helped the satire avoid the deadness of a lecture written by somebody who had never wanted anything expensive. The music performed a similar trick. Pop, rock, new wave, electro, soul and talk radio made the period feel coherent without making every inhabitant listen to the same thing. The game could sell a fantasy of the eighties and make fun of the people selling that fantasy, sometimes within the same drive. Vice City was released in 2002, looking back at 1986. The distance was sixteen years. GTA VI is arriving twenty-four years after Vice City, with more than twice as much distance from 1986 as the original game had. Nostalgia has had time to develop nostalgia. That arithmetic matters because Vice City's atmosphere now comes to players through two memories: the decade it depicted, and the period when they first played it. A modern Vice City cannot reproduce that by adding pink lights. Some of the glow belongs to an old television, a particular room and the absence of adult responsibilities. The game had limits. Its ethnic gang caricatures can make its supposedly expansive city feel small-minded. Its treatment of women often reduces them to scenery, temptation or a joke. Calling the setting satirical does not settle whether an individual gag has observed anything worth laughing at. Even so, Vice City made a lasting discovery. A GTA city could become memorable because its parts belonged together. Its strongest identity came from the relationship between the light, the music, the vehicles and Tommy's appetite for ownership. More activities would have meant little if they had broken that mood. 4. San Andreas: home becomes an entire state If Vice City was a beautifully dressed argument for excess, San Andreas brought a removal van. Released in 2004 and set in 1992, it followed Carl “CJ” Johnson home to Los Santos after his mother's murder. Family obligations, a weakened neighbourhood gang and corrupt police established a more personal starting point than Tommy's missing investment. The game drew on the cultural world of films such as Boyz n the Hood and Menace II Society , while its Los Angeles references included gang conflict and the history surrounding the 1992 unrest. CJ has a home that matters before the player begins buying anything. That gives his story a different emotional centre. Where Tommy wants to acquire a city, CJ has to decide what he owes the place he left. The eventual journey through Los Santos, San Fierro, Las Venturas and the spaces between them expands into something much stranger than that premise initially suggests. Street drama gives way to rural escapades, elaborate criminal operations and increasingly outrageous machinery. The tonal lurch can be wonderful. It can also make the opening's human stakes feel as though they have been packed away for later. San Andreas sometimes handles narrative escalation like a child explaining a dream: and then there was a casino, and then the military, and then you could fly. It works as often as it does because CJ remains personable. His exasperation makes a useful companion to the player's own. He gives the enormous game somebody to come back to. Mechanically, San Andreas chased an unusually broad idea of inhabiting a character. Food, exercise, body shape, clothing, haircuts, skills and relationships could affect the experience. Swimming and climbing expanded how you moved. Gang territory made parts of Los Santos contested space. There were bicycles, aircraft and long journeys into places that felt distant from the starting neighbourhood. Some of these systems were richer in possibility than in practice. A stat can encourage attachment, or it can ask you to perform maintenance before you are allowed to enjoy yourself. CJ's body gave player choices a visible consequence, but being told to improve a capability could also reveal how quickly immersion becomes homework. The geography had a deeper effect. Rural roads, forests and desert provided contrast. Distance gave arrival a sense of occasion. San Fierro felt like somewhere you had travelled to, with a different pace and shape, rather than another set of streets unlocked on the same commute. The radio helped carry those changes. Radio Los Santos grounded the West Coast rap identity, while K-Rose, K-DST and Radio X broadened the musical America surrounding it. Country music could accompany a stretch of open road; alternative rock could change the mood of another journey. A large map became several overlapping cultural spaces. San Andreas is therefore a useful rebuke to the idea that density always beats scale, or scale always beats density. Its expansiveness worked because the places differed. A hundred extra kilometres of interchangeable motorway would not have done the same job. The scandal that swallowed the conversation The game launched near the end of 2004, amid arguments about what blockbuster games could depict and who was actually buying them. The following year's Hot Coffee controversy transformed those arguments. The important detail is that the sexual material was present but disabled in the shipped software. The modification exposed it; it did not simply invent the content from nothing. The ESRB changed the rating to Adults Only, retailers pulled copies, and a revised Mature-rated edition followed. In 2006, the FTC announced a settlement over allegations that relevant content had not been disclosed properly. The comic irony is obvious: an industry and political culture already familiar with the game's extensive violence became convulsed by a hidden sex minigame. But reducing the whole episode to American prudishness misses the substantive ratings issue. Parents and retailers were relying on a description of what the product contained. The dispute was also about the accuracy of that description. It helped make San Andreas a cultural object people argued about without necessarily understanding what playing it involved. CJ's family, the state's musical variety and its odd experiments in character embodiment had to compete for attention with something most ordinary players had never seen. GTA was becoming so notorious that its reputation could obscure the game itself. 5. The pocket GTAs tried more than they get credit for The numbered entries dominate the history. The portable games deserve room because they tested which parts of GTA were essential when the hardware could not do everything. GTA Advance, 2004: the alternative route Released in the same year as San Andreas, GTA Advance returned to an overhead view on Game Boy Advance. Digital Eclipse built an original Liberty City story around Mike , whose plans to leave crime with his associate Vinnie collapse into a revenge plot. In a market being shown the scale of San Andreas, its compromises were easy to notice. The setting and mission patterns echoed GTA III, while the hardware narrowed how the city could be presented. It was a separate game, though, rather than a tiny port of the year's console release. Its historical value is partly that coexistence. For a while, GTA could mean both a sprawling console production and a more modest interpretation designed for another machine. The brand had not yet become synonymous with a single development event capable of swallowing a decade. Liberty City Stories, 2005: the city fits in a bag Liberty City Stories made the more immediately spectacular handheld argument: a recognisable 3D GTA city could run on PSP. Set in 1998, it follows Toni Cipriani back into the Leone family's work. Liberty City is familiar enough to create recognition, but earlier enough in its history for streets, relationships and power to sit differently. The story returns to mob obligation, career advancement and the difficulty of pleasing people whose preferred management technique is murder. Its compact mission rhythm suited portable play, even where the underlying design remained familiar. Radio preserved much of the sense of occupying a place rather than visiting a succession of levels. Released in the year of Hot Coffee, it also made the separation between an adult game and an adult-sized machine impossible to maintain. GTA could now accompany you on public transport. Everyone else on the bus would have to supply their own moral crisis. Vice City Stories, 2006: empire-building has a family cost Set in 1984, Vice City Stories centres on Victor Vance , whose attempt to support his family through military service goes disastrously wrong. His brother Lance helps connect this earlier story to Vice City's familiar world. Victor is an interestingly uncomfortable fit for GTA. He objects to the criminal world while repeatedly doing what it demands. That tension can communicate entrapment; it can also make the character seem less coherent than the game wants him to be. Contemporary reviews noticed the problem. The later series would revisit it with much greater ambition in Niko Bellic. Its criminal-business system is the more useful forgotten inheritance. Businesses could be established, developed and fought over. Acquisition was attached to a contested city, making empire-building more active than simply collecting revenue from a completed property. The musical period-setting remained central, and Phil Collins appeared as himself. It is difficult to imagine a more specific measure of the series' cultural reach than a game about criminal entrepreneurship making room for an actual Phil Collins performance. Stories also hints at the kind of future GTA could choose: revisit a strong location with another protagonist and a different social position. A new camera angle on a city can be more revealing than another island attached to it. 6. GTA IV: the American dream answers the door in its underwear GTA IV arrived in April 2008 , and its Liberty City offered a different sort of promise. Niko Bellic , an Eastern European war veteran, comes to America carrying trauma and unfinished business. His cousin Roman has advertised an enviable new life. The reality involves an unglamorous apartment, a taxi business and debts. Roman has, in effect, been maintaining a highly selective social feed by telephone. The joke has affection behind it. Roman's exaggerations conceal hope as well as embarrassment. Niko can be funny, loyal and frightening within the same conversation. These are people with enough warmth to make their circumstances matter. That warmth distinguishes IV's disillusionment from a general declaration that everybody is awful. Liberty City's promise is hollow, but friendship is not automatically meaningless. The game leaves you something to lose. Its reputation as the sombre GTA is justified, though incomplete. Brucie exists. A city containing Brucie cannot reasonably claim to have abolished farce. Fewer toys, more weight Compared with San Andreas, IV removed or narrowed many activities and systems. There was less scope for body transformation and no equivalent journey across three cities and their countryside. The emphasis shifted towards a denser urban setting, physical detail, cover-based combat, a more involved phone and social life, and online multiplayer. The cars felt heavier. Braking became an opinion you needed to express early. Bodies and vehicles reacted with a physicality that could produce either ugly comedy or an unexpectedly uncomfortable sense of impact. Those choices served the setting. Niko's Liberty City resists you. Traffic is traffic; a corner requires attention; a gunfight can feel messy rather than merely stylish. The game asks you to spend more time inside an ordinary urban life, even when that life has an extraordinary ammunition budget. Not every demand improved the experience. Friendships made the supporting cast more present, but the requests could become irritating. A relationship system is doing something peculiar when the player starts regarding an invitation to socialise as an attack on their remaining free time. Then there is Niko's central contradiction. He wants distance from violence, yet the game repeatedly uses his ability to inflict it as the engine of progress. Some of that is deliberate: his skills keep returning him to the world he hopes to escape. Some is the old GTA mission structure straining under a more serious character. Players can deepen the mismatch by treating free roam as an extended atrocity exhibition. The story cannot account for everything you do between scenes. Niko's dramatic life and the player's recreational behaviour sometimes inhabit neighbouring apartments and refuse to speak. Still, IV's ambitions matter. It asked a blockbuster audience to inhabit someone for whom arriving in America did not mean becoming important. Its Liberty City could make opportunity feel physically near and socially inaccessible. You could drive past the life you wanted without getting any closer to it. A game released into 2008 It is tempting to make IV sound like a direct response to the financial crash. The dates require more restraint. The US recession had begun in December 2007, according to the NBER's later dating. IV launched the following April, months before Lehman Brothers collapsed in September. A game of this size was not written in response to events that happened after it shipped. Its timing nevertheless changed the resonance of its story. A city built around money, ambition and unequal chances arrived while the real economy was moving towards disaster. The gap between the sales pitch and lived experience was becoming difficult to ignore outside the game, too. Meanwhile, GTA itself was prospering spectacularly. Take-Two reported roughly six million copies sold to consumers and more than $500 million in estimated retail sales in the first week. A story about the unreliability of American opportunity had become a demonstration of the entertainment industry's considerable opportunities. The radio made Liberty City feel inhabited by different communities. Russian-language music, reggae, hip-hop, rock and ambient selections offered more than a generic New York mood. Choosing a station could change which city's inhabitants seemed nearest to you. This is one reason later soundtrack changes matter. In 2018, Rockstar confirmed that expiring licences would remove music from IV and its episodes, with a substantial effect on Vladivostok FM. A patched game could preserve the streets while altering part of their cultural memory. The map remained. The drive was different. 7. The 2009 games found three more ways to inhabit Liberty City The Lost and Damned: belonging can be a trap Johnny Klebitz approaches Liberty City through the Lost motorcycle club. His conflict with its returning leader, Billy Grey, gives The Lost and Damned a more focused concern than becoming rich: what happens when loyalty to a group becomes loyalty to its worst decisions? Its motorcycles, gang presence and harder musical identity give the same urban space another rhythm. Riding with a club changes the image of arrival. Niko often looks like someone trying to enter a world; Johnny looks like someone struggling to preserve the world he already has. The tragedy lies in how little romantic freedom the biker ideal finally offers. The open road can still lead back to the same obligations, grudges and destructive people.
