Owning a leather jacket does not make a dysfunctional organisation less dysfunctional. The Ballad of Gay Tony: loyalty with better lighting The Ballad of Gay Tony moves through Luis Lopez , his partnership with nightclub owner Tony Prince, celebrity culture and the expensive lunacy of people such as Yusuf Amir. Parachutes, extravagant missions and nightclub life restore a degree of showmanship that some players missed in IV. Tony's sexuality is part of the story's world, but his relationship with Luis gives the episode more to work with than a title designed to cause a conversation. Luis has to navigate affection, exasperation, business and danger. He is protecting a person whose capacity for self-sabotage makes the job unusually demanding. The game can be loud and ridiculous while allowing that bond to matter. It supplies a particularly useful answer to the idea that GTA must choose between feeling something and blowing something up. The explosion improves when you care who is standing nearby. Together, the episodes form one of Rockstar's best experiments. Incidents and characters intersect, giving the impression of a city containing several stories rather than waiting exclusively for one protagonist. The same location becomes poorer, richer, more intimate or more absurd depending on who takes you through it. For a series now burdened by the expectation that each new entry should rebuild the industry, these shorter works remain an appealing precedent. A city can sustain more than one substantial story. The next project need not begin by moving the coastline. Chinatown Wars: the spreadsheet is contraband Chinatown Wars , first released for Nintendo DS in 2009, made an apparently backward-looking camera into a fresh design choice. Huang Lee arrives in Liberty City carrying a family sword, is ambushed and becomes entangled in Triad succession and betrayal. Comic-style scenes and touchscreen interactions establish a different presentation from IV's performances. The crucial system is drug trading. Buying cheaply, following market opportunities and selling elsewhere give you reasons to cross the city that arise from its economy. Stock in your possession changes what you stand to lose when the police become interested. It is a nasty little commercial simulation, and unusually effective GTA design. The money is attached to decisions. The journey has stakes before a character phones to announce them. Its wanted system also rewards knocking pursuing police vehicles out of action at lower wanted levels, putting more of the escape into what you do during a chase. The device-specific interactions can be fussy, but the game repeatedly tries to make the player participate rather than watch. The release context was revealing. The DS's huge audience and GTA's huge name did not guarantee an immediate sales triumph. Contemporary reports described a disappointing US opening, and Nintendo later publicly discussed its frustration with the game's commercial performance. That should not be inflated into a definitive explanation of lifetime sales, or evidence that adult games could never work on Nintendo hardware. It does show that acclaim, brand recognition and platform reach are different things. Chinatown Wars remains valuable because its solutions were specific to its format. Bigger GTA was not its only ambition. 8. GTA V: three men, one very expensive identity crisis GTA V launched on 17 September 2013 , at the end of the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 generation. It went on to pass $1 billion in retail sales within three days. By then the franchise was a major entertainment event before anybody had played the new release. GTA III had surprised people. V had to satisfy a world that expected to be astonished on schedule. Its solution was partly structural: Michael, Franklin and Trevor offered three positions within the same Southern Californian economy. Michael has the house, pool and money. He remains unhappy. Franklin wants a route out of small-time work and a neighbourhood future that seems already mapped out. Trevor operates with a mixture of grievance, cruelty and freedom that makes him both magnetic and exhausting. Switching between them changes geography, class position and temperament, sometimes in the middle of a mission. Michael is especially useful to the series' argument. Vice City lets you earn the mansion. V asks you to visit the man inside it. He has acquired the lifestyle and now needs an audience for his dissatisfaction. Franklin gives the story its clearest route of ascent, but too often becomes the reasonable person standing between more aggressively written personalities. Trevor brings the chaos some players expect from GTA into the authored story itself. His volatility closes part of the gap between a supposedly reluctant protagonist and a player who wants to turn a junction into an insurance event. It creates other problems. Once atrocity is a regular means of establishing character, escalation can exhaust itself. Shock eventually needs something underneath it. Otherwise the game is just pressing harder on a doorbell everybody has stopped answering. The heist becomes the organising fantasy V's heists give its criminal careers a compelling shared purpose. Planning, selecting approaches and moving between characters make a robbery feel like a coordinated production. The player gets several jobs in the same action film. The lighter, more accessible driving and the return of a broad city-and-countryside environment support a sunnier, more elastic game than IV. Los Santos and Blaine County can accommodate an urban commute, a desert disaster and a scenic excursion without asking them to feel like the same experience. The limitation is how much apparent planning remains under authorial control. You choose within a designed structure. The city outside offers improvisation; the spectacular mission often requires its machinery to run in a particular order. The better the production becomes, the more conspicuous its barriers can feel. America discovers it can film itself V also arrived at a useful cultural hinge. Pew found that a majority of American adults owned smartphones in 2013: 56 per cent. Self-presentation, social platforms and access to the internet were becoming ordinary features of daily life on a much wider scale. V's technology companies, entertainment culture, paparazzi and personal brands belong to that environment. Its Los Santos wants to be seen. Even failure benefits from suitable coverage. The game is often sharpest about people who convert insecurity into products or power. It is less effective when every person enters a scene already carrying the entire joke about them. Constant contempt can flatten a society until its absurdity stops being surprising. Its women suffer especially from that narrowness. Too many are written mainly to irritate, expose a man's frustrations or decorate an environment. Carolyn Petit's contemporary GameSpot review praised the game's achievements while criticising its misogyny and confused politics. These objections were present at launch; they have not been retroactively invented by people who arrived too late to understand the fun. There is also the torture mission. The scene can be read as attacking the usefulness and moral evasions of state violence, but the game makes the player perform the violence before delivering its critique. That is a deliberate, troubling construction. It is fair to ask whether the disgust serves the argument, or whether the argument is being asked to excuse another exercise in provocation. The music learns to follow the mission V's score added another layer to the series' musical identity. Tangerine Dream, Woody Jackson, The Alchemist and Oh No contributed to the original score, with DJ Shadow involved in shaping its soundtrack presentation. Radio could keep defining the world around you while composed music shaped the immediate action. A chase now had the city in one ear and a thriller gathering momentum in the other. That expansion makes music's importance even clearer. GTA is unusually good at giving players memories that are half action and half song. You may forget which mission paid for a car. You remember what was playing when you drove it into the sea. 9. GTA Online: the empire becomes your employer GTA Online launched on 1 October 2013 , two weeks after V. Its opening was beset by connection and progression problems, with Rockstar publishing updates as it tried to stabilise the service. That matters to the retrospective. Online did not arrive fully formed as the indestructible money-making institution later history can make it resemble. It grew through additions and revisions. The original cooperative Heists update arrived in March 2015; Cayo Perico followed in December 2020 and allowed its heist to be tackled solo as well as with others. Over time, Los Santos became a place to accumulate businesses, vehicles, properties, routines and shared memories. The audience was creating continuity that did not depend on a new authored protagonist. This fulfilled a long-standing GTA possibility. The city could be a social setting. Friends could turn a well-designed operation into an appalling rescue attempt, with the resulting failure more memorable than a clean completion. The cost was a different relationship with money. In a conventional GTA campaign, acquisition tends to move you towards an eventual state of abundance. In Online, a continuing catalogue of desirable things gives abundance somewhere else to go. Businesses, requirements, payouts and purchasable GTA$ can make the pursuit of freedom feel like managing an expanding portfolio of obligations. The joke writes itself: the series spent years mocking American consumerism, then offered a persistent world in which your criminal ambitions could be accelerated at checkout. That does not make every transaction exploitative or every session a chore. Online has supplied enormous pleasure and sustained relationships. It does make monetisation part of the experience's meaning. When a game jokes about greed, the way it sells you things belongs in the conversation. Why people wanted to play ordinary jobs inside GTA Roleplay communities revealed another appetite. A player might want to become a paramedic, mechanic, officer or small-time operator and maintain relationships inside a city, rather than pursue the next increase in destructive capability. In August 2023, Cfx.re, the team behind FiveM and RedM, officially joined Rockstar. That establishes a real relationship between the company and major roleplay infrastructure. It does not, by itself, confirm how VI's multiplayer will operate. The lesson is still useful. People can want more life in a GTA city without wanting more ammunition. A reliable neighbourhood, a small business or a reputation can give an ordinary street enormous significance. The series began by letting you disrupt a city. Some players have spent years finding ways to belong to one. 10. The games changed. So did the company selling them A retrospective that stops at the software risks making GTA seem like an unbroken stream of ideas from an unchanged group of people. It is a large, collaborative production, and its personnel have changed. Dan Houser left Rockstar in 2020. Leslie Benzies and Lazlow are other prominent figures from earlier GTA eras who departed. Recognising their contributions is reasonable. Declaring that a vast studio's future can be calculated from one departure is considerably less so. The work between GTA V and VI also included Red Dead Redemption 2 . Thirteen years between numbered GTA releases does not mean thirteen years spent solely on the same game. Nor can the gap simply be explained as Rockstar discovering that Online made money and locking the writers in a cupboard. Success does, however, change the pressure on a new release. A franchise expected to sustain a large audience for years faces different incentives from one turning out a strange handheld experiment. Financial scale can buy extraordinary craftsmanship while making risk more expensive to approve. Preserving the earlier games has exposed another problem. The Trilogy: The Definitive Edition launched in November 2021 with technical and presentation issues serious enough for Rockstar to issue an apology and announce improvements. A new version can increase availability while weakening the atmosphere people wanted to revisit. Alongside the soundtrack alterations in IV, it raises a question the franchise's future should not evade: what does it mean to preserve a GTA? Its atmosphere depends on lighting, weather, voices, music, visual clutter and small incongruities. A cleaner texture does not necessarily preserve those relationships. And there are the people making it all. The approach to VI's launch includes an employment dispute over Rockstar's dismissal of workers in the UK and Canada. The union alleges anti-union action; Rockstar disputes that and says the dismissals concerned confidentiality breaches. Reporting in October describes tribunal proceedings, not a final ruling resolving those competing accounts. The contradiction is uncomfortable without requiring an invented verdict. GTA is expert at finding comedy in powerful organisations. The organisation producing GTA should receive the same scrutiny as any other employer. 11. What GTA VI has actually shown us The return to Vice City is an attractive hook, but the public material describes a broader project: contemporary Leonida , with Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos at its centre. Rockstar's premise puts the pair inside a criminal conspiracy after an apparently straightforward score goes wrong. The important change from 2002 is time. VI is returning to a place associated with nostalgia while setting its story in the contemporary world. The city can no longer rely on the eighties to supply a safely completed cultural identity. A criminal partnership, with somewhere to go wrong Rockstar describes Jason as having grown up around criminals, served in the Army and drifted into drug-running work in the Keys. Lucia has recently left prison and wants a better life. Their relationship offers each a possible route forward. That is an especially promising centre for GTA. The series is very good at writing unstable business relationships. A romantic partnership introduces a different set of questions: what do these people owe each other, what do they conceal, and what happens when a good decision for one threatens both? The appeal is intimacy. A betrayal need not involve an entire criminal empire to matter. It may be enough that somebody you trust has lied about the money. Lucia is also a major change in the authored leading cast. Calling her GTA's first playable woman would erase the optional women in the original PC game and the female characters players can create in Online. Her significance is as a central, extensively written female lead in the modern cinematic series. That distinction gives the writers an opportunity to change who gets to have an inner life. It does not require Lucia to become a model citizen. A GTA protagonist can be selfish, cruel, funny and wrong. The improvement would be letting a woman possess the same range of dramatic possibilities that the men have enjoyed. Florida has more to offer than a compilation of arrests Rockstar has introduced locations beyond Vice City, including Leonida Keys, Grassrivers, Port Gellhorn, Ambrosia and Mount Kalaga . Its published cast includes people involved in music, property, robbery, smuggling and conspiracy-minded online life. The potential is geographic and social contrast. Wealth, tourism, industrial decline, wetlands, small communities and entertainment ambition can create different relationships to the same state. The danger is treating everything outside the glamorous centre as a supply of eccentric strangers to laugh at. Rockstar's research account is encouraging here. Aaron Garbut has described trips through Miami and the Keys, aerial reference work and time spent with local people. Rupert Humphries has discussed choosing durable targets for satire rather than chasing short-lived memes. Those are statements of intent. Their value will depend on whether Leonida feels observed at human scale. A crowd can contain a lot of polygons and very few people. We have moved beyond the first two trailers The public record now includes An Extended Look , released on 27 August 2026, alongside press previews. Rockstar identifies the showcase as footage captured on PS5. Contemporary coverage describes a nearly twenty-seven-minute presentation combining narrative sequences, locations and stretches of play, including shootouts, pursuits and leisure activities. That is substantial promotional evidence. It still cannot tell us how consistently the complete game will behave over dozens of hours. A demonstration can show an interaction working; it cannot establish how quickly the player will exhaust its variations. More interesting than a tally of activities are Rockstar's comments about mission flexibility . Rob Nelson has described opening up routes where possible and trying to keep systems such as pursuits consistent between missions and free roam. The examples reported include multiple exits from a tower block and a getaway that can continue without following its suggested optimal route. That addresses a longstanding fault line in the series. It suggests Rockstar knows the difference between showing the player something spectacular and letting the player make something happen. We will need the released game to judge how far it has gone. Nelson has also said money will matter more to progression, including moments when players need to earn cash through activities such as stealing cars or robberies before continuing the story. There is an excellent version of that idea. You need money; the city offers several risky opportunities; you choose one; the consequences become your story. Chinatown Wars already demonstrated how an economy can create reasons to move. There is a tedious version, too. The next interesting mission is waiting, but first you must repeat a reliable cash-producing action until the number is large enough. A requirement to earn money becomes meaningful through the decisions it creates. Poverty alone is not a gameplay system, as several billion people could confirm. Stealing a car is becoming a decision again The reported changes reach the activity on the box. Nelson has described tools and progression governing access to some parked vehicles, while carjacking a driver remains an option. A phone app can provide information about a vehicle's security and value. That could make looking at a car more interesting than immediately acquiring it. Is it worth the risk, do you have what you need, and what happens if somebody notices? The possibility of making a poor choice is useful here. A theft game benefits from the occasional theft being a bad idea. The wanted system is also being described in terms of information. According to Nelson's reported comments, crimes require a witness or alarm to reach the police. Preview coverage identifies recognition of clothing, faces, vehicles and the pair being together, alongside a return to a six-star maximum. A pursuit can become more interesting if the police know something specific that you can do something about. Changing vehicles, breaking sight lines and moving through alleys could offer decisions beyond outrunning the nearest patrol car. Whether that information stays legible to the player will matter as much as its complexity. For the driving itself, Nelson has pitched a combination of IV's sense of weight and V's accessibility. That is an appealing promise, and remains a developer's description rather than an independent verdict from someone holding the controller. Refuelling has also appeared in preview reporting, with a brief fill-up sequence. Its value will depend less on the existence of a petrol station than on when the game makes you need one. Running low during an improvised escape could create a story. Interrupting an enjoyable drive for routine maintenance could simply interrupt an enjoyable drive. GTA has been negotiating this balance since Gary Penn complained about the original game's excessive simulation. The newest music news belongs in the picture The musical plans are clearer than they were when the first trailer sent everyone back to Tom Petty. October's announcements include radio hosts and stations spanning Latin music, African music, metal, pop, Southern rap and country, with names including Bad Bunny, RaiNao, Burna Boy, Robyn, Trick Daddy and Trina. On 15 October, Pitchfork reported Rockstar's reveal that Justice composed the original score , alongside news of the launch trailer and music from the game's album. These are different layers of the soundtrack. The original score, songs made for an accompanying album, and the tracks available across in-game stations should not be collapsed into one number. An album track count is not the total number of songs in the game. The artistic test is the old one. Does a station sound like part of a place? Can the radio suggest a community, an argument or a history? Celebrity names may attract the headline, but the pleasure of GTA radio often comes from a song you did not know, introduced by somebody you would cross the street to avoid. What the announcements cannot settle The current official release page lists PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. A specific PC launch date should be treated as unconfirmed unless Rockstar announces it; October reporting about a possible PC window is reporting, not a platform announcement. Likewise, the future multiplayer economy, the long-term place of roleplay, the full scope of interiors and the quality of individual systems should not be reconstructed from rumour lists. A visible building is not a promise that you can enter it. Two protagonists do not automatically mean cooperative story play. We have enough real information to discuss VI intelligently. There is no need to promote every plausible wish into a feature. 12. What the next GTA should make possible The history suggests more useful expectations than “everything, but bigger.” Let a failed plan become a good story GTA's finest free-roam comedy comes from a system absorbing a mistake. A minor collision becomes an argument; an argument attracts police; escape requires abandoning the vehicle you meant to keep. More of that resilience inside missions would be a genuine advance. A getaway should be able to become a different getaway. A surviving witness should sometimes create a complication rather than invalidate the scene. A player who solves a problem in an unexpected, believable way should not always be escorted back to the approved solution. There will still be reasons to script an encounter tightly. A whole game needs rhythm, and performances need staging. The opportunity is to choose carefully where control matters and where a little disorder could improve the scene. Give wealth a scale we can feel Money works when spending it reveals a priority. Do you replace a damaged car, improve a safe place, buy equipment for a riskier job or help somebody whose favour you might need? The sums do not need to grow indefinitely. The early struggle for something modest can be more engaging than a late purchase that barely affects how you play. GTA has repeatedly made the climb vivid and abundance comparatively shapeless. For Jason and Lucia, shared money could also expose character. Two people can agree that they need a better life while disagreeing completely about what one looks like. Humphries has described the contemporary American dream in more modest terms: a home and freedom from debt, rather than extravagant success. There is considerable satirical potential in a world where the opening ambition of a criminal epic resembles the target on a mortgage calculator. Make the relationship worth the journey A convincing partnership needs unremarkable moments. Familiar jokes. Small disagreements. The ease of sitting beside someone when neither has anything useful to say. GTA already spends a lot of time in cars. That is an ideal space for intimacy. People can explain themselves badly, change the subject, argue about music and reveal what a grand confession would conceal. The worst outcome would be a romance that exists only between gunfights, announced through dramatic declarations while the player does unrelated work. The best would let affection alter how ordinary play feels. A risky decision becomes different when somebody whose company you enjoy is in the passenger seat. Find sharper targets than the person nearest the camera Contemporary satire faces a practical problem: reality can produce a more absurd story before a game has finished rendering its joke. The answer is observation. There is plenty to say about how money buys innocence, how platforms reward humiliation, how precarious people sell success and how powerful people recast consequences as persecution. The mechanisms endure longer than a particular viral clip. GTA also needs people who do more than embody the joke. IV's Roman remains funny because optimism and self-deception coexist with affection. Luis and Tony work because loyalty complicates exasperation. A whole city of loud idiots can be entertaining for an hour. Eventually somebody needs to make you care whether they get home. The satire should also survive a glance at the checkout screen. A new Online can offer spectacular toys without making every evening a negotiation with an economy designed to consume it. Keep a future for the smaller story The main release can be enormous. The franchise's future should have room for work that is more concentrated. A Leonida story from another class position. A new business system attached to a small cast. An episode that examines one corner of the map properly. The Lost and Damned, Gay Tony and Chinatown Wars show that a GTA can distinguish itself through focus, viewpoint and design rather than a larger promotional number. A city this expensive to create ought to be good for more than one kind of visit. The road back to Vice City Across GTA's history, the same criminal fantasy has kept changing its address. The original games offered the pleasure of disrupting a system. GTA III let us inhabit the disruption. Vice City made ownership irresistible. San Andreas gave ambition a home to answer to. IV asked what opportunity meant to somebody who had arrived too late and brought too much with him. V put the successful man beside the aspirant and the man who had abandoned most pretence. Online made the pursuit continue after the story should have ended. VI's opportunity is to make all that scale answer to two people. It can give us the spectacular state, the crowded beach, the wildlife, the music and the terrible decisions. The test is whether the details produce a place worth spending time in, and whether the people at its centre make leaving the next mission waiting feel like part of the experience. For all its money and cultural weight, GTA still needs to understand the appeal of a stolen car with a good song playing. We will probably crash it before the chorus. It would be nice to care who we crash it with. Sources and further reading The article's historical interpretation and future-facing judgments are editorial analysis. The notes below support the release history, reported facts and attributed statements. Original games are the underlying works discussed; contemporary reviews are used to recover how their features and reception were described at the time. Research checked 16 October 2026.

title: House of X/Powers of X Review: Xavier's Dream Gets Complicated
description: A review of Hickman's X-Men reinvention: Krakoa, Xavier's grey morality, the Quiet Council, remarkable art and the possibilities of a mutant nation.
body: Charles Xavier has spent a great deal of his publishing life explaining what the future should look like. In House of X/Powers of X , he finally arrives with something more substantial than an aspiration. There is a place. There is a plan. There are terms. And there is that helmet, which does very little to suggest that questions will be taken from the floor. I loved these books. I loved the scale of their ideas, the confidence with which they rearrange familiar relationships, and the sense that the X-Men have acquired a future worth arguing about. The political maturity appealed to me as much as the revelations. Jonathan Hickman gives mutant survival an institutional shape, then lets the people inside those institutions remain difficult, ambitious and capable of deceiving one another. The result makes it possible to feel exhilarated by what the mutants are building while wondering who has authorised the builders. Xavier, especially, becomes fascinating in that uncomfortable space. This is a combined review of the two interlocking 2019 miniseries. The opening sections avoid their major revelations. A clearly marked, closed spoiler section below discusses the full story. Later books receive a short, separately labelled recommendation section because the wider Krakoa era develops several of the things I enjoy most, particularly the Quiet Council and Arakko. A new country changes the question The X-Men's familiar struggle is exhausting by design. They save people who fear them. They ask to belong in a world that keeps finding reasons to exclude them. Their school offers shelter, but a school can be attacked. Their heroism is visible, but gratitude rarely becomes security. Krakoa changes the conditions of that struggle. Mutants establish a nation on a living island. They have territory, access controls, resources and a diplomatic proposition. The outside world has to respond to an organised political presence, rather than deciding whether it likes the latest group of costumed people on the evening news. That shift is enormously satisfying. It gives the X-Men room to think beyond surviving the next attack. What does safety require? Who belongs? What will other governments demand? What happens when people with incompatible histories have to share the same future? Hickman's writing allows those questions to coexist. Krakoa can offer something precious and still require scrutiny. Its critics can identify genuine problems without making every hostility toward mutants reasonable. A reader does not have to hand in their enthusiasm at the first sign of a moral complication. That is the maturity I responded to. The story takes a persecuted people's desire for security seriously, including the compromises that emerge when desire becomes policy. Its characters have reasons to want the island to succeed. Their reasons do not automatically make every decision defensible. House of X builds the present; Powers of X changes its meaning House of X and Powers of X work together as one twelve-issue narrative. House gives Krakoa its immediate presence: the island, the new arrangements and the people making them real. Powers widens the field, moving through different periods and making apparently settled information less comfortable. The alternating structure gives the reader two kinds of momentum. One comes from wanting to see the new society work. The other comes from wanting to understand why the story has arranged its history in this particular way. Each answer can change the terms of the first question. This is a large part of the pleasure. Hickman's revelations reorganise what you have already read. Returning to an earlier scene can expose a different motive beneath a conversation that initially seemed straightforward. The books reward attention without requiring a reader to arrive carrying an encyclopaedia. The data pages help make that possible. They offer definitions, classifications and diagrams where a conversation would otherwise have to stop and explain an entire system. They also make the world feel administered. Someone has decided what belongs in a category, what deserves a chart and what information is worth recording. Even an apparently neutral explanation contributes to the atmosphere of a society being designed. Read the books in their intended interleaved order. The chronology is a narrative device; untangling it before the first read would sacrifice some of the experience the structure is built to produce. The artists make an enormous idea feel inhabitable Pepe Larraz and R.B. Silva deserve their names alongside Hickman's whenever these books come up. Larraz gives House of X a world that can feel lush, strange and inviting, while preserving the unease of encounters in which someone clearly holds more power than the person opposite them. The island needs to feel like somewhere a person might want to live. Otherwise its political promise would remain an abstract claim. Silva's Powers of X has a different challenge: allowing the reader to follow unfamiliar settings, bodies and technologies as the scale expands. Clean visual storytelling makes the speculative ambition readable. There is a difference between making a future mysterious and leaving the reader unable to tell what happened in a panel. Marte Gracia's colour work helps bind these different spaces into a coherent experience, with David Curiel also contributing colours. Clayton Cowles's lettering and Tom Muller's design belong to the same achievement. The visual identity is unusually assured, from the organic world of the island to the disciplined presentation of information. The book looks as though its new order has already commissioned a complete set of stationery. That is both reassuring and faintly alarming. Most of all, the art gives the ideas a seductive surface. You can understand the attraction of Krakoa before considering the terms of admission. A purely ominous island would let us make up our minds too quickly. Why Xavier is the most interesting person in the room Xavier's ambiguity is one of the reasons this reinvention works so well for me. He has long been capable of withholding information and deciding that other people need only part of the truth. Here, that tendency acquires a far larger field of operation. His confidence can be comforting. Someone has thought ahead. Someone is refusing to accept the old pattern of catastrophe as inevitable. But confidence also makes it harder to know when conviction has become an exemption from accountability. The helmet reinforces the effect. Xavier is recognisable, yet access to his face is restricted. Other people must interpret the voice, the posture and the assurances. It is a striking visual choice for a man whose project asks so many people to trust his judgement. I find him more compelling when the book leaves that trust unsettled. I can want his plan to work without wanting his judgement to become the constitution. The possibility that he is doing something necessary makes the problem harder. So does the possibility that he knows it. The verdict, before the revelations House of X/Powers of X gave me the excitement of discovering that familiar characters could still move into unfamiliar territory. Its politics, speculative scale and formal design all contribute to that feeling. The books ask the X-Men to organise a future, and the change makes their old conflicts newly productive. They are demanding in places. Some concepts arrive before their purpose becomes clear; parts of the cast serve the architecture more than an intimate character arc. Those are useful expectations to set for another reader, rather than reservations that meaningfully diminished my enjoyment. I was happy to meet the books on those terms. The twelve issues tell the founding story while opening questions that later comics pursue. You can appreciate their construction as a single work, but you will finish with a strong invitation to keep reading. For me, that invitation was earned. If your interest in the X-Men includes difficult leadership, uneasy alliances and the consequences of power, this is an exceptional place to spend time. Let the books introduce their world before looking up the answers. Beyond these books: the Council and Arakko Some of what I enjoy most about the wider era develops after House of X/Powers of X . Arakko's expanded cast and political culture belong primarily to later stories. They should not be credited to these twelve issues as though the whole development is already here. What HoX/PoX provides is the foundation and appetite for an X-Men world with more than one way to organise mutant life. For readers drawn to the same aspects, these are destinations within the later era, not a complete consecutive reading order: Hickman's X-Men, starting with the 2019 series: the immediate expansion of the new world. Follow its collection notes when it reaches crossovers. X of Swords: the major next step for Arakko and its people. Read the event in its own chapter order rather than collecting only issues with X-Men on the cover. Planet-Size X-Men #1: an important bridge toward the setting developed in X-Men Red . Read it after X of Swords and with its Hellfire Gala context. Immortal X-Men by Kieron Gillen and Lucas Werneck: the strongest destination for more Quiet Council politics. It starts later, after the status-quo changes of Inferno ; follow that bridge before beginning. X-Men Red by Al Ewing, beginning with Stefano Caselli on art: the destination for Arakko, Storm and a different political culture. It is also a later entry, rather than the issue immediately following HoX/PoX. That breadth is part of the original books' success. They create a setting capable of sustaining disagreements between people who all have a stake in its future. The X-Men can fight over what kind of society to become, as well as whether they will be permitted to exist. I loved being given that possibility. I loved that the people promising it could still make me uneasy. A better future is a powerful thing to offer. These books leave me interested in the people asking for my trust, and alert to the terms. Reading the original twelve issues The standard combined collection interleaves the two titles. For single issues, use this sequence: House of X #1 Powers of X #1 House of X #2 Powers of X #2 Powers of X #3 House of X #3 House of X #4 Powers of X #4 House of X #5 Powers of X #5 House of X #6 Powers of X #6 Notice the consecutive Powers #2–3 and House #3–4. Simply alternating matching issue numbers changes the intended order. Marvel's later Chronological Edition is a different arrangement; save that experiment for a reread. The X in Powers of X is pronounced “ten”. For the next author route, read our Jonathan Hickman feature and Hickman reading guide . For more fresh approaches to familiar heroes, explore our Absolute Universe and Dark Knights of Steel reading guides.

title: The Best Jonathan Hickman Comics: What Happens When the Plan Fails
description: From Fantastic Four and Secret Wars to House of X and East of West, the Hickman comics that make the strongest case for his ambition.
body: Jonathan Hickman has a reputation for making comics that require diagrams. This is unfair. Sometimes he supplies the diagrams himself. There are charts, organisational hierarchies, ominous symbols, impossible histories and people who appear to have been hired specifically to say that everything is proceeding according to plan. Often, everything is proceeding according to three incompatible plans. Somewhere in the building, Reed Richards has neglected dinner. The reputation catches the surface of the work and misses its most compelling feature. Hickman's best comics put faith in human intelligence, then ask what intelligent people will excuse once they believe everyone else's survival depends on them. Their scale is cosmic. Their recurring problem is painfully recognisable: someone has decided that being the cleverest person in the room also makes them the person entitled to lock the door. That tension connects a remarkably varied body of work. Fantastic Four makes a family the necessary check on genius. New Avengers examines the moral collapse of an elite convinced it has no alternative. House of X/Powers of X gives an endangered people the machinery of a nation and invites us to admire it, fear for it and scrutinise it simultaneously. East of West imagines a political order that has turned apocalypse into an appointment. These are the essential books, chosen for the force of their ideas, their visual storytelling and how well their ambitions become drama. The order below is an editorial ranking, with the interconnected Avengers saga treated as one undertaking. Major endings and the central HoX/PoX revelations stay unspoiled. For purchases and sequence, use the Jonathan Hickman reading guide ; for other writers, visit our five-author starting list . 1. Fantastic Four and FF: the family comes first The strongest all-round Hickman work. With Dale Eaglesham, Steve Epting, Nick Dragotta and a substantial artistic ensemble, Hickman turns Marvel's first family into an argument about what progress is for. The collected route covers Dark Reign: Fantastic Four , his main-series run and FF , the Future Foundation companion book. Reed Richards wants to solve problems on the largest possible scale. This is admirable until solving everything becomes a reason to spend less time with the people who make any of it matter. The Council of Reeds gives that temptation a particularly sharp form: intelligence can multiply across realities while emotional judgment stays stubbornly scarce. Hickman understands that Reed's defining flaw does not have to be stupidity disguised as genius. He can be extraordinarily capable and still need Sue to tell him that a useful discovery is not an adequate substitute for a husband. Family becomes a way of testing ambition against actual obligations. A universe full of theoretical beneficiaries does not release you from the child standing in front of you. The Future Foundation broadens that argument. A school of unusual children makes the future something adults must prepare other people to inhabit, rather than a private monument to their own brilliance. Valeria's confidence is funny because she belongs to this household; it is disquieting because the household already contains a cautionary example of intelligence outrunning judgment. Franklin gives the story another scale of vulnerability and possibility. Ben supplies the emotional weight that a lesser version of this run would try to replace with another galactic war. The artists keep its two scales in contact. Eaglesham's physical solidity makes Reed's cosmic work feel like something a body must live through. Epting's faces and staging give grief room to register. Dragotta brings a different energy to the children and the extraordinary spaces around them. The Future Foundation's visual identity makes intellectual cooperation look exciting without requiring every member to acquire matching shoulder armour. There is a substantial price of admission. Locations, factions and future promises accumulate. Reading only the issues branded Fantastic Four eventually means missing half the conversation. But the apparent sprawl has an emotional centre clear enough to hold it: can a man who wants to save everyone remember how to belong to someone? This is the best first sustained encounter with Hickman because it demonstrates both his architecture and his warmth. It also improves the experience of the later Marvel saga. Understanding Reed as a father, husband and friend gives his relationship with Doctor Doom a force that no multiverse glossary can supply. 2. Avengers, New Avengers and Secret Wars: intelligence meets its limit The great large-scale undertaking. Avengers expands the public team; New Avengers follows a secret group confronting incursions, collisions between universes that make survival an intolerable problem. Infinity intersects the two series. Time Runs Out carries them toward Secret Wars in 2015. Marvel's own collections gather these linked strands, and the eventual event is nine issues by Hickman and Esad Ribić. The public Avengers project is built on recruitment and the belief that a sufficiently capable team can meet a sufficiently large threat. The private Illuminati story asks what happens when the threat makes that belief inadequate. Between them sits the difference between a heroic institution's stated purpose and the decisions made in its closed meetings. Hickman gives the Illuminati a problem that cannot be dismissed by announcing that superheroes should simply be nicer. He then refuses to let the difficulty of their situation cleanse their choices. The most frightening developments arrive when deliberation becomes routine. Something that would once have seemed unthinkable turns into the next item on the agenda. Black Panther and Namor are crucial because their responsibilities cannot be reduced to an abstract equation. They bring nations, histories and incompatible obligations into the room. Captain America's presence tests the claim that moral refusal is merely an indulgence for people who have not understood the stakes. The series makes room for both the force and the limits of that objection. Its most effective repetition is structural. A plan is made. Its inadequacy emerges. Another plan requires an additional compromise. The heroes accumulate knowledge faster than they recover moral ground. Apocalypse acquires the atmosphere of a committee that keeps extending its emergency powers. The art is essential to that escalation. Jerome Opeña helps establish the enormous scope of the early Avengers material; Steve Epting makes the rooms of New Avengers feel heavy with unspoken decisions. Across the run, artists including Mike Deodato and Stefano Caselli give its confrontations different textures. This is a collaborative visual undertaking, with the inevitable unevenness of a long monthly schedule. Secret Wars finally gives Ribić space to make the consequences monumental. His figures have the weight of damaged sculpture, while Ive Svorcina's colour helps the world feel ancient, unstable and lived in. The setting could have become an excuse to display alternate costumes. Its dramatic centre remains authority: who claims the right to preserve a world, what that preservation costs, and whether creation can be disentangled from possession. Some of the journey is forbidding. Secondary characters can function more as components than people. Several scenes gain meaning only after later issues. Readers who want every chapter to provide immediate closure may find the run exhausting. Its strongest defence is the destination: the scale contracts at the moment that matters, until the future of everything can be understood through a few deeply personal relationships. Read the main Secret Wars series if you want a shorter encounter. Read the Avengers road to it if you want its ethical pressure. Add Fantastic Four/FF first if you want the fullest emotional argument. You do not need every tie-in with a Battleworld logo; the multiverse has already suffered enough administration. 3. House of X/Powers of X: a revolution with terms and conditions The most electrifying reinvention. Two six-issue series, with Pepe Larraz and R.B. Silva and colour led by Marte Gracia, establish a new political reality for mutants. They form one twelve-part work and depend on their intended interleaving; Marvel explicitly describes both as essential. The remarkable decision is to give the X-Men's familiar argument a change of position. Mutants have spent decades asking whether they will be permitted to exist safely. Here, their leaders begin making offers, setting conditions and constructing institutions. Readers accustomed to treating the X-Men as a besieged school encounter the much stranger prospect of a people learning how to wield power. That movement is exhilarating because the desperation behind it is legible. It is unsettling because legitimate fear does not make a government's every decision legitimate. Hickman lets the language of liberation coexist with secrecy, hierarchy and the confidence of leaders who have made extraordinary decisions on everyone else's behalf. The data pages are part of that effect. They make a new society feel as though it possesses rules, supply chains, doctrines and a functioning information system. At the same time, an official document always raises a question: who gets to write the official account? The form makes certainty attractive before the narrative asks us to inspect its authors. Larraz gives the new homeland a physical generosity that makes the promise feel worth defending. Silva handles temporal and technological complexity without reducing it to a procession of diagrams. Gracia's colour gives the two books a shared sensual vocabulary. The future is persuasive because it looks like somewhere people might actually want to live. For a reader who loved HoX/PoX, the next Hickman book depends on which pleasure mattered most. Choose Fantastic Four for the emotional consequences of an ambitious plan. Choose New Avengers for the hidden cost of elite decision-making. Choose East of West for rival powers caught in an enormous historical machine. The qualification matters: HoX/PoX is a brilliant foundation, not the complete history of the Krakoan era. Hickman's later X-Men and Inferno develop his contribution, but many writers shape the wider line and its eventual conclusion. Selling the whole era as a single author novel misrepresents what the books are. Our dedicated HoX/PoX review examines why the opening works so well without pretending it seals every question it raises. 4. East of West: the apocalypse is a political project The strongest independent epic. Hickman and Nick Dragotta, with colour by Frank Martin, build an alternate America of competing nations, prophecy, technology and the Horsemen of the Apocalypse. The main series is complete at forty-five issues, collected in ten standard volumes and a full-story compendium. The early density can be intimidating. There are people to identify, territorial claims to understand and factions that appear to have spent the previous century rehearsing how best to betray one another. An initial reading can feel like arriving late to the least reassuring diplomatic summit in history. Dragotta is the reason that density becomes a world rather than a dossier. His silhouettes make powerful figures instantly legible. A pause before violence can feel as charged as the violence itself. Martin's colour lets barren spaces, technological grandeur and sudden brutality coexist without flattening the book into a uniform apocalypse brown. At its centre is Death, whose personal attachments interfere with the role the world expects him to perform. That gives the political scale an emotional lever. History says events must proceed in one direction; a person has reasons to want otherwise. The question is whether those reasons can withstand institutions built to make the catastrophe happen. Its leaders also expose a recurring Hickman concern: systems can become self-justifying. A prophecy provides a reason to act, and the resulting actions provide evidence that the prophecy was right. The story's political orders do not merely anticipate disaster. They invest in it. The book is less immediately welcoming than Fantastic Four and more consistently cruel. Some of its enormous cast remains more memorable as an image than as a fully developed person. But its original setting allows consequences and relationships to acquire a finality that shared superhero universes can rarely sustain. It offers a major Hickman construction with an actual ending and no request that you first familiarise yourself with forty years of somebody else's mutants. 5. Secret Warriors: the organisational chart has teeth The essential espionage book. Hickman, working from a project launched with Brian Michael Bendis, follows Nick Fury and a younger covert team through a war between secret organisations. Stefano Caselli and Alessandro Vitti are major artistic voices. The original run ends at #28. The series is a useful bridge between Hickman's reputation for intricate plotting and the experience of reading him. Its hierarchies, hidden connections and loyalties are recognisable as spy-fiction machinery. You may not know what every symbol means, but you understand that the man withholding information probably has a contingency plan for your funeral. Fury's competence is part of the attraction and part of the danger. His capacity to see several moves ahead does not make being one of his pieces a healthy profession. The younger characters give that imbalance a cost. From the commander's perspective, a sacrifice may be necessary. From the recruit's perspective, necessity still arrives with a name and a body. Caselli brings clarity and urgency to the team material; Vitti's harsher textures suit the story's attrition. The run makes the logistics of espionage feel consequential without losing the appeal of people doing dangerous things extremely well. Its weaknesses are those of a compressed conspiracy story. Revelations can run ahead of emotional processing, and some supporting players never become as substantial as the machinery around them. Even so, it is a more manageable demonstration of the long game than the entire Avengers project, and a good choice for readers who prefer betrayal at human scale to metaphysics at universal scale. 6. Decorum: the visual argument The best reminder that Hickman's work is not merely a matter of plot. With Mike Huddleston, Decorum offers an eight-issue science-fiction story involving assassins, a courier and extraordinary institutions. Its defining attraction is the breadth of Huddleston's image-making. Painted grandeur, graphic abstraction, spare drawing and extravagant design can share the same book. The shifts in register help distinguish kinds of experience, power and space. A world can look overwhelming because the person entering it has been overwhelmed; another can feel precise and remote because its inhabitants have learned to treat living things as manageable material. That range gives the central contrast between ordinary vulnerability and extraordinary professional capability a visual life. Expertise looks seductive. So does belonging to an organisation with beautiful clothes and terrifying standards. The book is interested in what passes from mentor to pupil besides technique. It is not the most emotionally rounded selection here. The setting sometimes appears ready to support a much larger story than the one we receive. But as a finite encounter with Hickman's design sensibility and a collaborator capable of answering it with remarkable invention, it earns its place. The other books worth knowing about The Nightly News matters because Hickman draws as well as writes it. Its aggressive page design and media satire make the later fascination with information systems easier to recognise. It is a sharper, angrier and more abrasive proposition than his family superhero work, rather than a necessary first step. S.H.I.E.L.D. , with Dustin Weaver, transforms historical geniuses into participants in Marvel's hidden cosmic history. Choose it for elaborate visual imagination and arguments about whether history has a predetermined end. Its two principal collections, Architects of Forever and The Human Machine , belong together; the shared acronym does not make it an ordinary Nick Fury mission. The Black Monday Murders , with Tomm Coker, deserves attention for making finance and occult horror feel like natural colleagues. Its material already published is compelling, but the publisher's catalogue lists the original run through #8 rather than a completed final movement. Coker discussed returning to conclude it in August 2026, but that intention is not a published ending. Readers seeking a finished story should choose East of West first and check for a confirmed final collection before buying on a promise of closure. Ultimate Spider-Man , launched in 2024 with Marco Checchetto and contributions from David Messina, is especially appealing if you want Hickman's interest in possible futures placed inside adult domestic life. This is a different Ultimate continuity from the original Brian Michael Bendis series. Marvel bills #24 as the end of this Hickman/Checchetto run; a cover label saying “Ultimate” does not mean an indefinitely continuing Hickman project. Why the diagrams keep leading back to people The fairest criticism of Hickman is that the machinery sometimes takes over. A revelation can be easier to admire than to feel. A character can enter a room as an interesting person and leave as a necessary part of a future chart. The density also rewards patience unevenly: an enormous payoff does not retroactively make every intervening conversation graceful. His best work succeeds by making those liabilities part of its subject. Plans promise to relieve people of uncertainty. They can also turn other people into things that fit. Again and again, the decisive question is what happens when a relationship resists the scheme: a family, an old friendship, a national obligation, a child who cannot be reduced to an expected role. Start with Fantastic Four/FF for the fullest expression of that idea. Start with House of X/Powers of X for its most concentrated shock. Take East of West if you want a complete original universe, or the Avengers saga if you want to watch a system exhaust every justification it has. The charts explain how the world is supposed to work. The people explain why it might deserve another chance. Sources and scope Publisher listings establish credits, issue counts and collection relationships. The rankings and interpretations are Fourth Frame's editorial judgments. This is a selected body-of-work assessment, not a complete bibliography; publication details were checked on 17 October 2026.

title: The Best Grant Morrison Comics: Strange Worlds, Human Hearts
description: All-Star Superman, Animal Man, Doom Patrol, New X-Men and more: the essential Grant Morrison comics and what makes their strangeness matter.
body: A living street. A superhero who borrows animal abilities. A cat, a dog and a rabbit turned into military hardware. A dying Superman trying to put his affairs in order. Grant Morrison's best comics do not share a sensible definition of sensible. They do share a moral instinct. A person can be strange, damaged, artificial, unfashionable or extremely difficult to explain at a dinner party and still deserve love. Often the institutions demanding that everyone become normal are far more frightening than the people who cannot comply. Morrison's reputation for difficulty is earned, but unevenly useful. Some works expect you to assemble connections across decades of superhero history. Others can break your heart in three issues. Advising everyone to begin with the most cryptic book is like recommending swimming lessons by pointing at the Atlantic. The strongest way into the work is through what each comic asks its artists and readers to do. Frank Quitely gives compassion a physical form. Chas Truog makes an ordinary family's world legible before its borders grow uncertain. Richard Case makes the impossible sufficiently concrete that it can become someone's home. Morrison supplies ideas that need those collaborators to become experiences. This is an editorial ranking of essential works, with major endings withheld. It favours achievement and range over a complete career inventory. The Grant Morrison reading guide separates approachable books from continuity-heavy projects; our writer starting list connects this feature to Hickman, Moore, Brubaker and Vaughan. 1. All-Star Superman: the extraordinary work of being kind The best first book and the strongest single recommendation. Morrison, Frank Quitely and Jamie Grant give Superman twelve issues in which to face his mortality. DC collects the entire series in one volume. You need familiarity with the broad idea of Superman, not a degree in Kryptonian genealogy. The impending end changes the meaning of the hero's power. Strength can accomplish extraordinary tasks, but it cannot make time irrelevant. The question becomes how someone with immense abilities chooses to use the time left to him. Morrison takes the exuberance of older Superman stories seriously. The impossible experiments, extravagant threats and strange relatives are part of the world through which his responsibilities must move. A smaller, more respectable version of that world would give him less to love. Quitely's contribution is particularly important when Clark Kent occupies the page. His posture changes what people see. Apparent awkwardness can conceal extraordinary attention to the people around him. The double identity becomes a performance made out of weight, shoulders, space and timing, rather than something a reader must politely overlook. The series repeatedly makes saving a person feel as consequential as confronting a cosmic danger. Its celebrated acts of reassurance work because the book has established a man who notices. Compassion is a use of attention before it becomes a demonstration of strength. Lex Luthor supplies the counterargument. Exceptional intelligence can become a prison when its owner interprets another person's existence as an insult. Superman's approaching death exposes the poverty of a life organised around defeating him. The contrast makes the story's optimism feel considered rather than automatic. Its episodic structure can initially seem loose. Some chapters feel like doors into stories the series does not have time to pursue. The accumulation is the point: a life becomes visible through obligations, unfinished work, old relationships and the things someone chooses to repair. By the end, the extravagance has acquired the intimacy of a farewell. 2. Animal Man: who is responsible for the pain? The clearest encounter with Morrison's ideas about fiction. The twenty-six-issue run, principally drawn by Chas Truog with Doug Hazlewood and other collaborators, starts with Buddy Baker trying to be a superhero while maintaining a family and taking animal suffering seriously. It develops into a much stranger examination of who controls a story. Its ordinary domestic footing is crucial. Buddy has bills, children and a marriage. His moral concerns create friction rather than automatically making him admirable. Because his life feels inhabited, the book can question its rules without treating that life as disposable. “The Coyote Gospel” is the early demonstration of what the series can do. Its shift in visual and narrative logic turns a familiar entertainment tradition into a question about suffering. The violence that one genre asks us to find funny can look unbearable from inside the victim's experience. That concern reaches beyond formal cleverness. A story can always arrange another ordeal for a character; an audience can always ask for greater stakes. Animal Man asks what desire is being satisfied and whose pain is being used to satisfy it. The book becomes most moving when an ingenious formal device produces an ethical problem that ingenuity cannot neatly solve. Truog's directness gives this development its foundation. The everyday world does not look as if it was designed solely to demonstrate a philosophical thesis. The drawings allow Buddy's bewilderment and concern to remain human when the narrative becomes increasingly unstable. Some of the topical material carries the texture of its late-1980s context. The changes in register will also frustrate readers who hoped for a straightforward animal-powered hero. But the run's endpoint has a rare quality: it makes the relationship between creator, character and reader feel like a matter of responsibility. Read it before reading explanations of it. 3. Doom Patrol: a home for people the world cannot categorise The essential long strange trip. Morrison's run begins at Doom Patrol #19 and continues through #63, with Doom Force Special #1 included in the omnibus. Richard Case is its defining artistic collaborator. The book's weirdness is not random decoration. It gives physical form to the experience of being told that your mind, body or identity makes you unfit for ordinary life. A person whose situation resists a simple category needs more than an invitation to become less inconvenient. Cliff Steele's robot body makes separation from ordinary human experience brutally literal. Crazy Jane's presentation is more complicated and should not be treated as clinical guidance, but the story's interest in trauma and fragmented experience helps distinguish her from a mere catalogue of powers. Danny the Street turns the idea of refuge into geography. Case's great achievement is consistency within impossibility. An absurd entity occupies space and interacts with other entities. That gives the characters a world to negotiate. Without that discipline, the book could dissolve into a collection of surreal descriptions waiting for someone to draw them. The antagonists also challenge the assumption that order must be good. Systems of classification and conformity can become violent when confronted with lives they cannot process. The Doom Patrol's solidarity matters because it is practical: these people keep trying to live alongside one another when conventional heroism has no useful instructions. The run is demanding, sometimes abrasive and very far from a tidy adventure series. Its treatments of trauma and bodily difference can be uncomfortable. Its lasting strength is the conviction that the misfits deserve a world, rather than an explanation for why they cannot belong to this one. 4. We3: three issues, almost no protection The most concentrated work. Morrison and Quitely's three-issue story follows three animals transformed into weapons and attempting to escape their intended function. Jamie Grant's colour and digital production help give its violence an unnerving precision. The animals' limited speech does an enormous amount of work. They do not need to become witty human personalities to earn the reader's concern. Their needs are immediate and comprehensible. The gap between that simplicity and the elaborate technology imposed on them is the story's wound. Quitely makes action feel distributed across time and space. Small panels and fragments isolate movements that a conventional splash page might compress into a single heroic image. The resulting spectacle is impressive, but it also makes bodies vulnerable. The reader experiences destructive capability alongside the fact that someone inside the machine is afraid. There is sentiment here, unapologetically. The book earns it through specificity rather than presenting generic animal innocence as a substitute for character. The creatures disagree, misunderstand and rely on one another. Their relationship is legible before the story asks you to mourn anything. The warning is simple: expect graphic violence and animal suffering . This is an easy continuity entry point, not an emotionally gentle one. If that material is a firm boundary, begin with All-Star Superman instead. 5. New X-Men: the school becomes a culture The most consequential Marvel reinvention in this selection. Beginning at #114, Morrison's run takes the X-Men through #154 and the 2001 annual. Frank Quitely establishes the new visual direction; artists including Igor Kordey, Phil Jimenez, Chris Bachalo and John Paul Leon contribute to the run. The central achievement is to imagine mutants as a developing culture. Xavier's school becomes a place with students whose bodies, tastes and anxieties cannot all be translated into glamorous combat roles. The difference between being a member of a super-team and belonging to a minority becomes more visible. That gives the adult cast a more difficult job. They must teach people to live in a world, not simply train future recruits. Emma Frost's presence is productive because her judgment, vanity and perceptiveness complicate the school's preferred account of itself. The students can expose contradictions that their teachers have grown accustomed to overlooking. The run is also willing to make familiar relationships awkward. Scott and Jean do not become uninteresting because readers recognise them. Their history makes the distance between them more painful. The book treats emotional habits as things that can fail under pressure, even when those habits have supported decades of stories. There are substantial qualifications. The visual changes between arcs are pronounced. Some revelations and portrayals remain divisive, and later continuity reworks parts of the material. Its sexual and body-horror elements are stronger than a new reader might expect from the franchise name. It belongs here because its ambition is social as well as spectacular. Read it alongside Hickman's House of X/Powers of X and an illuminating contrast emerges: Morrison foregrounds the strange, often untidy experience of a mutant culture, while Hickman's opening concentrates on the institutional force of mutant nationhood. Neither supplies the final word on what the X-Men can mean. 6. Batman: an inheritance large enough to change The most rewarding commitment for established superhero readers. Morrison's Batman project moves from Batman and Son and Batman R.I.P. through Batman and Robin , The Return of Bruce Wayne and Batman Incorporated . Andy Kubert, Tony S. Daniel, Frank Quitely, Frazer Irving, Yanick Paquette and Chris Burnham are among its key artists. Its generous premise is that Batman's strange history can belong to the character. The bizarre adventures do not all have to be filed away as embarrassing evidence of an era before the franchise discovered rain. They can become experiences Bruce has absorbed and prepared for. This makes Batman's identity expansive, but the most appealing movement is the change in partnership. Dick Grayson as Batman and Damian Wayne as Robin invert familiar expectations. The older partner brings relative warmth and social ease; the younger one brings severity, suspicion and the belief that he already knows everything worth knowing. The friction supplies both comedy and genuine growth. The Batman idea also becomes transmissible. It can survive an absence, move between people and operate internationally. That raises questions about whether Bruce is building something that can outgrow him or merely enlarging his personal mission. The family remains the most reliable test of his answer. The difficulty is structural. Final Crisis supplies a major transition that the Batman collections do not simply replace. The Return of Bruce Wayne and Batman and Robin overlap. A bare list of trade titles can give a newcomer a misleading sense of straightforward sequence. Our guide explains a manageable collected route and what remains outside it. For a focused sample, read Batman and Robin: Batman Reborn , accepting its changed status quo. For the full statement, begin earlier and follow the arc through Batman Incorporated . The reward is a Batman expansive enough to contain both impossible preparation and the uncomfortable work of being a father. The advanced shelf: The Invisibles, Seven Soldiers and Final Crisis The Invisibles is the major countercultural project: conspiracy, identity, liberation and reality itself made unstable across three volumes of numbering. Its collaborators include Steve Yeowell, Jill Thompson and Phil Jimenez. It is a substantial adult commitment, and the first volume contains disturbing violence and sexual material. Choose it because that investigation interests you, not because someone has mistaken confusion for a qualification exam. Seven Soldiers builds an ensemble event from an opening special, seven four-issue miniseries and a closing special. Its pleasures include watching separate lives contribute to a shared outcome without becoming an ordinary team adventure. Use the assembled collection's sequence. J.H. Williams III and the individual miniseries artists are indispensable to how the architecture becomes readable. Final Crisis is rewarding when its mythic compression meets a reader who already enjoys DC's history. It is an unnecessarily difficult sales pitch for someone who just wants to understand why Morrison matters. The fact that We3 and All-Star Superman exist should retire that particular initiation ritual. What the strange worlds make possible Morrison can be uneven. Formal ambition can move faster than explanation, and emotional transitions occasionally arrive with less preparation than the conceptual machinery. Some readers will find the work liberating; others will feel that they are doing too much of the assembly themselves. But the finest books make a persuasive case that imaginative freedom is an ethical resource. If a street can be a person, the category of person has expanded. If Superman can be both cosmically powerful and attentive to a stranger, kindness need not be an apology for weakness. If an animal built to kill can want a home, its assigned function has failed to describe its life. Start with All-Star Superman . Follow with Animal Man or, if you can bear its subject, We3 . Then let your interests decide how strange the next room should be. There are plenty of doors. Morrison's best work wants more people to fit through them.
